checklist.footerText: Autonomous agents that pick up cards and write code. When you're curious:
checklist.stepBoardIntro: A board is where the work becomes visible. Instead of holding everything in your head or scattered across chats, each piece of work becomes a card that moves through columns as it progresses.
checklist.stepBoardBullet1: Cards carry the detail — description, priority, discussion and history.
checklist.stepBoardBullet2: Columns come typed from the start, so progress reads at a glance.
checklist.stepBoardBullet3: Everything else in Backplane — context, notes, repositories — hangs off a board.
checklist.stepContextIntro: Project context is the background someone needs before they can help. Written down once, it saves you from re-explaining the project to every teammate and every agent that joins later.
checklist.stepContextBullet1: Objectives and constraints stay next to the work they shape.
checklist.stepContextBullet2: Search reaches it, so answers surface instead of being asked for.
checklist.stepContextBullet3: Agents read it first, which makes their output match your intent.
checklist.stepNotesIntro: Notes and resources keep the knowledge around a project from scattering. Runbooks, decisions and links live beside the boards they belong to instead of in a document nobody can find.
checklist.stepNotesBullet1: Pin what matters so it stays at the top for everyone.
checklist.stepNotesBullet2: Attach notes to a board or a card, or keep them workspace-wide.
checklist.stepChannelsIntro: Channels give a conversation a home. Decisions and threads stay attached to the workspace rather than disappearing into a chat history nobody can search later.
checklist.stepChannelsBullet1: Each channel gathers the discussion around one topic or audience.
checklist.stepChannelsBullet2: Anyone joining later can read how a decision was reached.
checklist.stepMembersIntro: Bringing teammates in is what turns a workspace into shared ground. Everyone sees the same boards, notes and channels, so the project stops living with one person.
checklist.stepMembersBullet1: Roles decide who can change what — invite as member, admin or viewer.
checklist.stepMembersBullet2: Teammates get the full picture, not a forwarded summary.
checklist.stepReposIntro: Linking a repository closes the loop between planning and code. Cards point at the codebase they change, and agents know where to work when they pick something up.
checklist.stepReposBullet1: Cards and commits stay connected to the same project.
checklist.stepReposBullet2: Runners need a linked repository before they can open a pull request.

Human keeps merging in your hands; the reconciler still lands the card after you merge.

discover.summary: Finds the next eligible card for this role and reserves it — the entry point of every role's run.
discover.whenToUse: As the first step of a role, to pull work using the stage's discover strategy (unassigned/rework, column scan, or label scan).
discover.gotcha: Params are ignored at runtime — discovery uses the stage's discover/filters/preconditions config, not the step's params. When no card matches, the role's run ends cleanly (idle), it does not error.

claim.summary: Takes ownership of the discovered card, opening an execution record the rest of the run logs against.
claim.whenToUse: Right after discover, before any step that does real work (LLM, git, notes) — nothing downstream can run without a claim.
claim.gotcha: `pipeline_role` is the canonical role key that discover's require_pipeline_role / skip_if_pipeline_role filters match on; set it or sibling roles can't coordinate. `participant_role` (hero/helper) is only a display hint now.

git_setup.summary: Prepares the working tree — clones the repo and creates or checks out the branch the LLM will edit.
git_setup.whenToUse: Before an LLM step that writes code, or before opening a PR; skip it for read-only roles (a reviewer that only comments).
git_setup.gotcha: `base_ref` must match what create_pr targets (integration_branch vs default_branch) or the PR silently retargets main and bypasses integration.

skills_setup.summary: Copies the board's bound workspace skills into the working tree so the coding agent can load them during the LLM step.
skills_setup.whenToUse: Between git_setup and an LLM step, so the materialized skills land inside the freshly prepared working tree.
skills_setup.gotcha: A board with no bound skills is a clean no-op — the assignment bundle carries no manifest and the step just passes through; it never fails the run over an empty set.

llm.summary: Runs the coding agent for a named stage with its authored prompt — the step that actually thinks, writes code, or judges.
llm.whenToUse: The core of most roles: implement, review, plan, reconcile. The `stage` names which prompt to load and which model tier applies.
llm.gotcha: It only branches the pipeline when post_process_kind is `produces_decision` (e.g. a reviewer's approve/request_changes); writes_code stages return no decision. With no authored prompt the stage soft-skips via the `no_prompt` branch — wire it for a graceful path.

sensor.summary: Runs a single programmatic check and branches on its pass/fail result — a deterministic gate, no LLM.
sensor.whenToUse: To guard a stage on an objective condition (tests green, a file exists, a threshold met) before proceeding.
sensor.gotcha: Returns the on_pass / on_fail string as the decision — wire both to real next steps or a fail silently dead-ends.

move_card.summary: Moves the card to a column by type (backlog/active/review/done/blocked) and ends the role's run for this card.
move_card.whenToUse: As a terminal step to hand the card to the next stage of the board (e.g. a planner moving a card to active).
move_card.gotcha: A force-blocked card is only allowed to move to `blocked` — any other target is skipped so a fail-move can't undo the cost-breaker park.

apply_label.summary: Adds a label to the card (idempotent — a no-op if already present).
apply_label.whenToUse: To stamp routing/audit signals other roles key on (e.g. `planned`, `needs-ui-validation`), usually chained before a move.
apply_label.gotcha: Deliberately NON-terminal so it can chain into a real terminal (apply_label → move_card). A label-add backend error is logged, not fatal — labels are bookkeeping.

remove_label.summary: Removes a label from the card and ends the run (no-op if absent).
remove_label.whenToUse: To clear a routing/state label once a stage is done with it (e.g. dropping a `rework` flag after a successful re-run).

create_note.summary: Writes a typed note onto the card (a review verdict, plan, or rework brief) and ends the run.
create_note.whenToUse: To persist an LLM step's structured output as durable board context the next role reads.
create_note.gotcha: `kind` is required (a closed-set note type) and `body_from` selects which LLM channel fills the body; an empty resolved body is a hard error, not a silent skip.

enqueue_for_merge.summary: Submits the card's PR to the backend merge queue and ends the run.
enqueue_for_merge.whenToUse: When merges are serialized through the platform queue rather than merged directly by the runner.
enqueue_for_merge.gotcha: On enqueue failure it errors to the walker — wire an on_failure or branch if you want fail-soft; the legacy swallow behavior is gone.

mcp_call.summary: Invokes a generic backend tool that has no dedicated kind of its own.
mcp_call.whenToUse: Only as an escape hatch — reach for a specialized kind (move_card, apply_label, create_note) first; they're better-typed and survive validation.
mcp_call.gotcha: The runner supports a closed set of tools; an unknown tool errors the run rather than no-op'ing.

create_fix_cards.summary: Reads the prior decision step's fix list and files one blocker card per finding against the source card.
create_fix_cards.whenToUse: In an auditor role (e.g. ui_validator) to turn a request_changes verdict into concrete follow-up work.
create_fix_cards.gotcha: On a request_changes verdict that filed zero fixes it synthesizes one umbrella card, so the source→fix dependency always exists — otherwise the auditor loops on the same unfixed card. Non-terminal: it chains into the verdict label swap.

branch.summary: Routes to a named next step by matching a variable's value against a case table — an explicit go-to.
branch.whenToUse: When you need to route on something the closed kinds don't emit (e.g. a custom mcp_call output).
branch.gotcha: Minimal expression language (${var}, ${last_decision}, or a literal); unknown values fall to cases['default'] then step.next. Not a real expression engine.

wake_role.summary: Clears sibling roles' idle cooldown so they pick up downstream work on the next tick instead of waiting out their backoff.
wake_role.whenToUse: After a handoff (e.g. planner → implementer) to make the next role react immediately rather than after its poll interval.
wake_role.gotcha: A silent no-op on a single-role runner and for unknown role names — it's a latency optimization, not a hard dependency.

create_pr.summary: Opens a pull request for the code the prior LLM step pushed.
create_pr.whenToUse: After a writes_code LLM step, in a role that ships via PR.
create_pr.gotcha: Base branch comes from the same resolver as git_setup — they must agree or the PR retargets the repo default and bypasses integration. Stores the PR url for downstream steps.

enable_auto_merge.summary: A retired no-op — kept in the registry only so old configs referencing it don't fail to start.
enable_auto_merge.whenToUse: Don't add it to new pipelines. Merges happen via the reviewer's explicit merge_pr after an approve verdict.
enable_auto_merge.gotcha: Does nothing at runtime: it depended on a GitHub-only feature and was dropped for the git-provider-agnostic north star.

merge_pr.summary: Merges the card's PR directly (or hands it to the merge queue when the workspace routes merges through the queue).
merge_pr.whenToUse: In a reviewer role, after an approve verdict, as the real merge path.
merge_pr.gotcha: A thin merge — it does NOT retry-on-rebase or route-to-blocked on failure; compose those via on_failure → create_note + move_card.

post_pr_review.summary: Mirrors the reviewer's verdict onto the PR itself via the forge (a GitHub review or a comment).
post_pr_review.whenToUse: After a review LLM step, to make the verdict visible on the PR, not just on the card.
post_pr_review.gotcha: Defaults the decision to the last decision step's output; fail-soft — skipped cleanly when the card has no PR or forge review is off, and gh errors are logged, not fatal.

ship.summary: The canonical end-of-stage step for a hero role — moves the card to its next column AND stamps PR/branch metadata onto it.
ship.whenToUse: As the terminal step of an implementer-style role that produced a PR (defaults the card to the review column).
ship.gotcha: Prefer ship over a bare move_card for hero roles: move_card only moves the card, ship also records the PR/branch footer the reviewer needs.

end.summary: An explicit no-op terminator that stops the run without any side effect.
end.whenToUse: To end a non-terminal step's branch cleanly (e.g. after an apply_label at the tail of a failure subtree) instead of relying on terminal-by-default.

columnType.summary: Column type drives runner behavior. Discover strategies filter cards by column type — renaming a column only changes its label, but changing its type re-routes the entire runner pipeline.
examples: backlog: where discover strategies look for new cards to claim.
active: work in progress; implementer writes code here.
review: awaiting reviewer tick; auto-merge arms against status checks.
done: terminal success state; the documentation owner may mark documented.
blocked: scheduler skips these cards until unblocked.

columnTypeChangeWarning.summary: Changing the type of a column that already holds cards may strand those cards — runners filtering by the old type will no longer pick them up. Move or relabel the cards first if you want them picked up under the new type.

kanbanCardAgentActive.summary: A runner is actively working this card right now. Click the robot to jump to the live execution detail.

kanbanCardAgentEligible.summary: A runner can work this card — an agent participant is assigned but no execution is in flight yet.

kanbanCardAgentTouched.summary: Last worked {{when}}. A runner has acted on this card before; no execution is in flight right now.

kanbanCardAwaitingPrompt.summary: A runner attempted a pipeline stage that has no prompt authored yet, so the run was skipped. Open the card's runner activity subtab to author the missing prompt.

budgetStatus.summary: Cumulative runner spend across the current period. Crosses the warning threshold at 80% of the configured budget; runners stop polling once the budget is fully exceeded until the next period or a manual reset.
examples: Per-runner cap: set on the runner itself; ignored if no budget is configured.
Workspace-wide accounting follows the model_pricing on workspace_config.

budgetPeriodReset.summary: Spend accumulates until the period rolls over. A new period zeros the spent_usd counter and unblocks polling; no manual reset is required once the new period begins.
examples: Mid-period spikes persist until rollover — manual override requires clearing the counter in workspace settings.
Budget exceeded mid-run stops new claims but does not kill already-started executions.

pipelineStageRole.summary: Free-form role name that identifies this stage across scheduling, prompts, and the observatory. Any text is valid — defaults (`implementer`, `reviewer`, `documentator`) are just starting points.
examples: Must be unique within the pipeline.
Referenced by prompt configs via (workspace, team, team_role, stage) — rename carefully.

pipelineDiscoverStrategy.summary: How this stage finds its next card: claim fresh/rework work anywhere, or pull from one specific column.

rows.label: Trigger
rows.value: unassigned_or_rework: missing participant OR rework flag  //  column_scan: card sitting in one column_type

rows.label: Column scope
rows.value: unassigned_or_rework: entire board  //  column_scan: single column_type (backlog/active/review/done/blocked)

rows.label: Rework behavior
rows.value: unassigned_or_rework: re-picks reviewer-rejected cards  //  column_scan: only sees cards currently in the target column

rows.label: Use when
rows.value: unassigned_or_rework: implementer-style, claims exclusive ownership  //  column_scan: reviewer or documentation-owner style, acts on a specific state

rows.label: Ignored fields
rows.value: unassigned_or_rework ignores column_type (field is disabled in the UI)

callouts.text: Default for most hero-style stages is unassigned_or_rework — it's the only strategy that re-picks cards a reviewer kicked back.
column_scan with an empty column_type never finds work — the stage will silently idle. Always pair column_scan with a concrete column_type.
Both strategies apply the stage's filters (require_git_repo, skip_if_participant_role, include_label, exclude_label) after the initial candidate set.

examples: A reviewer-style stage scanning the review column for cards ready to be critiqued.
A documentation-owner stage walking the done column to write release notes after ship.
An implementer-style stage using unassigned_or_rework to claim any card that lost its owner or was bounced back.

sections.title: unassigned_or_rework
sections.summary: Board-wide hunt for cards that have no participant with this role, plus any card a reviewer returned to rework/active.
examples: Claims exclusive ownership via participant.role = hero.
Survives reviewer rejection: the card re-enters the candidate pool automatically.

callouts.text: This is the right pick when the stage should own a card from start to finish.

sections.title: column_scan
sections.summary: Walks one column (column_type) in position order and takes the first card passing the filters.
examples: Pair with column_type: review for reviewer-style stages.
Pair with column_type: done for documentation-owner stages that run after ship.

callouts.text: Leaving column_type blank makes this strategy a no-op — the scheduler finds nothing and moves on.

pipelineClaimParticipantRole.summary: Display-only hint for how this step's actor relates to the card (hero = the primary owner, helper = a secondary contributor). The canonical role used by discover filters is the step's pipeline role, not this field.

rows.label: hero
rows.value: Primary owner of the card for this stage.

rows.label: helper
rows.value: Secondary contributor alongside an existing owner.

callouts.text: Legacy field — kept as a UI hint. Discover filters key on the pipeline role, so leaving this blank is fine.

pipelineGitAction.summary: Git operation performed before the LLM runs. `create_branch` cuts a feature branch from main; `checkout_pr_branch` switches to an existing PR branch; `none` skips git entirely for roles that don't touch code.
examples: create_branch: implementer starting new work.
checkout_pr_branch: reviewer examining the hero's branch.
none: researcher/planner roles that only read context.

pipelineLLMStage.summary: The stage token IS the prompt selector. The runtime looks up a prompt config by (workspace, team, team_role, stage) — change this string and you change which prompt the runner runs. Unrelated to `claim.execution_action`, which is just a telemetry label.
examples: Seeded tokens with built-in prompts: implement, review, document, plan, research.
Custom token (e.g. `triage`): create a matching prompt config first, otherwise the stage will skip with `no_prompt`.
Renaming the stage string on an existing pipeline silently swaps which prompt loads — author the new prompt before you rename.

tools.summary: Tools the LLM is allowed to call during this stage. Passed to `claude -p --allowedTools`. Runtime access depends on the client: Claude Code / Codex expose built-ins by default, but the stage will fail if the operator's CLI doesn't have the tool wired.
examples: Valaris MCP tools are always available to runners using the Backplane runner runtime.
Claude Code built-ins (Read, Bash, WebSearch…) only work if the launching client is Claude Code or an equivalent with matching tool names.
For other MCP servers, paste the exact tool id — we can't verify it's wired on the client side.

claudeBuiltins.summary: Tools commonly exposed by coding agents like Claude Code and Codex. Safe to assume when the operator is running one of those clients — otherwise the stage will fail at runtime when the tool isn't found.
examples: Read / Write / Edit / MultiEdit: file edits in the repo.
Bash / Glob / Grep: shell + search in the repo.
WebSearch / WebFetch: external lookup (requires internet).

valarisMcp.summary: Tools served by the Valaris MCP server. Always available to the runner runtime — this is how runners interact with boards, cards, notes, and approvals.
examples: `mcp__valaris__get_card` is the canonical way to read card details — prefer it over inferring from context.
`mcp__valaris__log_execution_update` lets the runner report progress mid-run, which the observer UI surfaces live.

other.summary: Tools from other MCP servers or a custom client. We can't list them — paste the exact tool id and make sure the operator's client is configured to expose it.
examples: Third-party MCP tools use the prefix `mcp__<server>__<tool>`.
If the runtime doesn't recognise the id, the stage fails at tool-call time.

toolBadge.summary: Tools currently allowlisted for this stage. Click the × to remove, or re-tick the checkbox below to restore. The runner passes this list verbatim to `claude -p --allowedTools` at launch.
examples: Hover a known tool to see its one-line purpose; custom ids render their raw string.
Removing the last built-in on a code-writing stage is how you accidentally ship a reviewer that can't read files.
Order doesn't matter — the runtime de-duplicates on startup.

columnType.summary: Which column_type this discover strategy scans. Disabled when strategy is `unassigned_or_rework` (that strategy works board-wide and ignores the field).

rows.label: backlog
rows.value: Where fresh cards land — implementer-style discover usually pulls from here via unassigned_or_rework.

rows.label: active
rows.value: In-progress work. Reviewer's rework loop returns cards here.

rows.label: review
rows.value: Awaiting reviewer verdict. Pair with strategy `column_scan` for review-style stages.

rows.label: done
rows.value: Terminal success. Documentation-owner stages walk this column after ship.

rows.label: (empty)
rows.value: No column_type pinned. With column_scan this is a silent no-op — the stage idles.

callouts.text: column_scan with an empty column_type never finds work. You can stare at the logs for a while before reaching that conclusion.
Renaming a column does not change its column_type — the type is semantic, the name is cosmetic.

includeLabel.summary: Only cards carrying this label are candidates. Leave empty to accept every card that passed the strategy and earlier filters. Useful for label-dispatched roles.
examples: Set to `role:researcher` on a researcher stage and the implementer won't fight for the card.
Labels are free-form strings. Typos are accepted and will silently exclude every card.

excludeLabel.summary: Cards carrying this label are rejected. Combines with include_label — include narrows, exclude subtracts.
examples: Set to `blocked-external` to skip cards waiting on a human.
Documentation-owner stages often exclude `documented` so they don't re-process the same card.

skipIfParticipantRole.summary: Cards already carrying a participant with this role are skipped. Keeps helper roles from stepping on each other and prevents a role from claiming a card it already owns.
examples: Reviewer stage sets this to `reviewer` so it only picks a given PR once per rework cycle.
Comma-separated to list multiple roles — the filter matches any.

callouts.text: Applies after the initial discover strategy — it narrows the candidate set, not the scan scope.

requireGitRepo.summary: Only considers cards whose board has at least one linked git repo. Flip on for any stage that runs `git.action`; the runner will fail fast if it claims a card without a repo.
examples: Implementer + reviewer stages should keep this on.
Planner / documentation-owner stages that don't touch git can leave it off.

requirePrUrl.summary: Only considers cards that already have a PR URL attached. This is the reviewer's honest gate — no PR, no review.
examples: Implementer sets the PR URL when it ships; reviewer picks up after that.
Set this to `false` and your reviewer will try to review cards that have nothing to review.

executionAction.summary: A free-text label stamped on the execution row for observability. The scheduler doesn't read it; the LLM doesn't read it. It's a tag for humans filtering the execution log.
examples: Conventional values: `implement_card`, `review_pr`, `document_card`, `plan_backlog`.
Rename freely — nothing breaks. It will not change which prompt loads (that's the LLM stage field).

callouts.text: Common confusion: this is NOT the prompt selector. The LLM stage field is the prompt selector.

branchPrefix.summary: Prefix applied to the feature branch name. Final branch is `{prefix}{card_id}` — keep a trailing slash or dash if you want a separator.
examples: `feat/` produces `feat/42`.
`agent/` is a common choice for runner branches, making them easy to filter on GitHub.

callouts.text: Force-push safety checks refuse any branch that doesn't start with this prefix. Change the prefix after the fact and old branches become immutable to this runner.

createPr.summary: Whether the runner opens a pull request after pushing. Off means the runner commits + pushes and stops; the operator (or another stage) opens the PR.
examples: Implementer stage: on — that's the whole point.
Rework-only stage that pushes to an existing branch: off, because the PR already exists.

forcePushOnRework.summary: When the card is flagged as rework, use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of a normal push. Required when the rework stage rewrites commits on the existing PR branch.
examples: Rework stages that squash or amend: on.
Stages that append a new commit to the same branch: off — a fast-forward push is enough.

callouts.text: Force-push refuses to touch `main` / `master`, and refuses branches that don't carry the configured branch_prefix. That's deliberate — losing a PR branch is cheap, losing main is not.

llmEnabled.summary: Whether this stage runs an LLM at all. When off, the stage is discover + claim + git + post-action only — useful for purely mechanical steps (e.g., move-column-and-wake-role).
examples: Off: a `tag_documented` stage that only adds a label to cards in Done.
On: `implementer`, `reviewer`, or `documentator` — any configured role that actually thinks.

approvalEnabled.summary: When the LLM emits `request_approval(...)` via MCP, the runner yields and the approval gate decides whether to proceed. Off: approval requests are ignored and the LLM runs as if every action were pre-cleared.
examples: Implementer stages that touch production config: on.
Read-only roles (researcher, reviewer): safely off — they don't emit approvals.

callouts.text: Risk score below AUTO_APPROVE_THRESHOLD auto-approves without a human — this gate is what routes the rest.

postProcessKind.summary: Declares what this stage's LLM call produces. The backend splices the matching tool-call imperative into the prompt — you don't hand-write 'Step N: Call create_note(...)' yourself.

rows.label: writes_code
rows.value: LLM edits files in the working tree; runner commits + pushes.

rows.label: produces_decision
rows.value: LLM returns a structured { decision, findings }; runner routes via on_success.branches.

rows.label: produces_note
rows.value: LLM returns findings; runner calls mcp__valaris__create_note on the card.

rows.label: mutates_backlog
rows.value: LLM calls MCP tools directly (plan_work, decompose_card, bulk_create_cards).

rows.label: (empty)
rows.value: No post-process. The runner takes the raw output verbatim — no automation, no routing, no note.

callouts.text: This is the magic. Pick a kind; the prompt writes itself the part most operators forget — the explicit tool-call imperative that actually makes the artifact happen.
Change this mid-flight and the next tick uses the new imperative. Cards that were already running keep the old one — no retroactive rewrite.
Leave empty only if you are writing the tool-call imperative directly in the prompt body. That works; it also means you're the one who has to remember it.

examples: writes_code: the implementer actually shipping a commit.
produces_decision: the reviewer emitting approve / request_changes.
produces_note: the documentation owner persisting release notes back on the card.
mutates_backlog: a custom decomposer splitting a card into subcards.

injectDirectives.summary: When on, board-level directive notes are pre-pended to the rendered prompt as a `=== PROJECT DIRECTIVES (MANDATORY) ===` block. Used to steer behavior without editing the prompt template — e.g. 'use Python 3.12', 'always write tests first'.
examples: Directives come from notes tagged `directive` on the board (workspace-level notes are not pulled).
Pinned notes are included alongside directives — pin the ones you want loud.
The injection happens at render time, not at save time — edit a directive note and the next tick picks it up.

callouts.text: Sonnet tends to treat injected directives as optional reference. If directive compliance is load-bearing for this role, pair inject_directives with Opus.

sensorsList.summary: Sensors run after the LLM call and decide whether the stage succeeded. Each sensor emits a pass / fail decision key that routes the on_success action via conditional branches, or falls through to on_failure on a miss.

rows.label: go-test
rows.value: Runs `go test ./...`; passes if exit 0.

rows.label: conflict-check
rows.value: Fails if the branch has merge conflicts with the default branch.

rows.label: pr-overlap
rows.value: Fails if another open PR already touches the same files.

callouts.text: The platform ships a handful of sensors; the catalog is agent-reported at runtime. If the picker only offers fallbacks, no runner has reported its catalog yet.
Config is a free-form JSON blob. Each sensor has its own accepted keys; invalid JSON is silently dropped rather than propagated, so double-check the textarea is clean before you save.

onSuccessAction.summary: What happens when the stage completes without error. Move the card, wake other roles, stamp labels, persist a note, or fan out on a decision key. Unconditional by default — flip `conditional` for branches.

rows.label: move_to_column_type
rows.value: Moves the card into the first column of that type. Leave empty to stay put.

rows.label: wake_roles
rows.value: Marks the named roles as wake-candidates for the scheduler's next tick.

rows.label: add_label / remove_label
rows.value: Free-form label mutations. Typos are accepted — the label will be created.

rows.label: unassign_self
rows.value: Removes this role's participant. Used when handing off to the next role.

rows.label: append_learning
rows.value: Appends reviewer findings to the board's definition for future runs.

callouts.text: wake_roles on a role that doesn't exist in this pipeline is silently ignored. If the `documentator` role isn't waking up after ship, double-check the spelling here.
Conditional branches read from the decision key in the LLM's structured output. No structured output, no branching — conditional becomes a dead switch.

onFailureAction.summary: What happens when the stage fails — exit code, LLM error, sensor miss, or approval denial. Typically moves the card to a rework column and unassigns the hero so the orchestrator can re-claim.
examples: Implementer on_failure: move_to_column_type=backlog, unassign=true.
Reviewer on_failure: move_to_column_type=active, create_review_note=true.

callouts.text: Failure doesn't retry the stage immediately. The scheduler applies min_failure_backoff_seconds before the next tick touches this role.
Leave this empty and the card sits where it is with the original participants intact. Sometimes that's right; usually it's a foot-gun.

wakeRoles.summary: Role names to wake on the scheduler's next tick. The scheduler only advances to a role when something asks for it; wake_roles is how one stage hands off to the next without polling.
examples: Implementer on_success.wake_roles = ["reviewer"] after opening a PR.
Reviewer approve-branch.wake_roles = ["documentator"] after merge.

callouts.text: wake_roles on a role that doesn't exist in this pipeline is silently ignored. If the `documentator` role isn't waking up after ship, double-check the spelling here.

conditionalAction.summary: Route the action by the LLM's decision key instead of a single unconditional step. Only meaningful when post_process_kind is `produces_decision` and the structured output includes a `decision` field.
examples: Reviewer: branches = { approve: { move_to_column_type: done, wake_roles: [documentator] }, request_changes: { move_to_column_type: active, unassign_self: true } }.
Decision key is matched verbatim. An unknown decision falls through to on_failure.

callouts.text: One-level nesting only in the UI. The engine accepts deeper nesting; the builder doesn't render it.

schedulingPriorityOrder.summary: Role execution order when mode is `priority`. The scheduler iterates left-to-right and picks the first role with claimable work. When mode is `round_robin`, this list is the rotation order.
examples: Typical order: [implementer, reviewer, documentator]. Reviewer fires only when the implementer has no new card to claim.
Drag to reorder. Removing a role from the list doesn't delete the stage — the scheduler auto-extends with missing roles at save time, appended to the end.

callouts.text: Leaving a role off the list is not a silent skip — the backend appends it on save. Your saved order may differ from what you typed; re-open the builder to see the canonical list.
Roles with no claimable work are put on a 4-minute idle cooldown so the scheduler doesn't burn CPU re-asking.

schedulingMode.summary: How the scheduler chooses which role runs each tick.

rows.label: priority
rows.value: Iterate priority_order left-to-right. First role with claimable work wins. Later roles never run while an earlier one has work.

rows.label: round_robin
rows.value: Rotate one role per tick through priority_order, skipping cooling roles. Each role gets fair turns regardless of backlog depth.

callouts.text: Priority is the right default — you usually want the implementer to drain the backlog before the reviewer wakes up.
Round-robin is the correct choice when you have multiple heavy roles that each pay for themselves. Under priority, lower-priority roles can starve.

pageSave.summary: Persist the draft to the backend. Validation runs client-side first; server-side validation runs on submit and can report errors the UI didn't catch.

callouts.text: Save uses optimistic concurrency. If another tab or operator saved a newer version while you were editing, save fails with a drift dialog — reload or override.
The backend canonicalizes on save (e.g. auto-extends scheduling.priority_order). Your local draft is re-seeded from the server response, so a successful save may quietly re-order fields.

pageExport.summary: Download the pipeline as a JSON file — the exact shape the backend stores. Useful for version-controlling a pipeline outside the UI, copying between workspaces, or pasting into an issue when you need help debugging it.
examples: The export is the full pipeline_config — stages, scheduling, version. Import is not wired yet; today the paste path is manual.
Filename defaults to `{workspace}.valaris.pipeline.json` — rename freely, the backend doesn't care.

pageDriftDialog.summary: Appears when another tab or teammate saved a newer pipeline version while you were editing. Reload pulls the latest and drops your draft; override force-saves your draft on top of the newer version.

callouts.text: Override wins the race. Whatever the other editor added will be replaced by your draft — including stages and roles they just created.
Reload is almost always the right call. If you're sure your draft is the authoritative one (you were the other editor, different tab), override.

pipelineLLMInjectDirectives.summary: When enabled, board-level directive notes are prepended to the rendered prompt at run time. Used to steer behavior without editing the prompt template itself — e.g., 'use Python 3.12' or 'always write tests first'.
examples: Directives come from notes tagged `directive` on the board.
Opus honors directives reliably; Sonnet tends to ignore them — prefer Opus when directive compliance matters.

pipelineContextSources.summary: Backend-rendered context blocks injected into this stage's LLM call. Each declared source is fetched server-side and exposed to the prompt under its alias. The prompt must reference it as {{ index .ContextSources "alias" }} — declaring a source here does nothing until the prompt references it (the prompt editor shows green/amber chips for this).

callouts.text: Sources are assembled at /next-assignment and shipped in the assignment bundle — code-controlled context, never LLM-fetched.
Declaring a source without referencing its alias in the prompt silently drops it. The Prompts page chips + inline warnings surface this.

pipelineToolPolicy.summary: Commands the coding agent is forbidden to run at this stage; protects the review gate. Each entry is a Bash prefix pattern, e.g. Bash(gh pr merge:*), enforced by the runner on both Claude Code and Codex (prefix match only — nested shells are backstopped by the server-side merge gates).

callouts.text: Enforced by the runner — denied patterns reach the coding agent as a deny-list (Claude Code disallowed tools, Codex execpolicy rules), so it can't run them directly at runtime.
Removing a git/merge deny entry lets the agent self-merge or force-push, bypassing the reviewer. Keep merge/force-push patterns denied on implementer-style stages.

pipelineStepOnFailure.summary: Where the walk jumps if THIS step throws at runtime. The executor routes to the named step instead of aborting the lifecycle — typically a cleanup subtree (drop the participant, apply a failure label). Leave it as (none) to let a failure abort the walk.

rows.label: On success
rows.value: Routing follows branches (if the step produced a decision) or next.

rows.label: On error
rows.value: Routing jumps to on_failure, if set; a failure inside the failure handler is not re-routed.

rows.label: (none)
rows.value: No handler: the step's error aborts the lifecycle for this card.

callouts.text: This is per-step error routing, independent of next/branches (the success path). A step can have both.
e.g. an LLM step might route on_failure to a step that unassigns the runner and labels the card so it isn't silently stuck.

pipelineLLMPostProcessKind.summary: Declares the shape of this LLM step's output so the executor can route the artifact correctly. It selects which post-run handler fires — commit/PR creation, decision parsing, note persistence, or backlog mutation — regardless of which role owns the step.

rows.label: writes_code
rows.value: Treats output as a code change: stages the working tree, commits, optionally opens a PR. (e.g. a build/implement step.)

rows.label: produces_decision
rows.value: Parses a structured verdict from the output and exposes it as a branchable decision token. (e.g. an approve/request_changes review step.)

rows.label: produces_note
rows.value: Persists the output verbatim as a card note of the kind a downstream create_note step expects. (e.g. a docs/summary step.)

rows.label: mutates_backlog
rows.value: Interprets output as backlog edits: creates or updates sibling cards via MCP. (e.g. a planning/decomposition step.)

callouts.text: Leave unset for a read-only step that produces no side-effect artifact (analysis fed only into context).

pipelineBuilderLlmStage.summary: A free-form stage token that pairs this LLM step with an authored prompt. The runner looks up the prompt by `${role}::${stage}`, so the token must match a prompt that exists in Prompts (or you author a new one). Any string is valid — it is just the join key.
examples: A token like `plan` resolves to the `${role}::plan` prompt for whatever role owns this step.
Two steps in the same role use distinct tokens (e.g. `scope` then `build`) to fire two different prompts.
Reusing a token across roles is fine — each role::token pair is a separate prompt.

callouts.text: If no prompt matches `${role}::${stage}`, the step runs with a minimal fallback (or errors) — the Prompts page flags unmatched tokens.

pipelineBuilderLlmProvider.summary: Which LLM backend runs this step. The Runner supports claude-cli and codex-cli; the Pipeline Builder currently exposes claude-cli, while Runner provider routing can select codex-cli.
examples: claude-cli: spawns the Claude Code CLI binary on the runner host.
codex-cli: spawns the Codex CLI through Runner provider routing.
anthropic-api / openai / gemini: planned direct-API providers.
local: planned escape hatch for self-hosted models (ollama, vLLM).

callouts.text: Source of truth: runner/internal/llm/provider.go. The Pipeline Builder dropdown is narrower than the Runner provider registry; disabled direct-API options are not runnable yet.

pipelineBuilderLlmModel.summary: Model tier resolved by the backend at dispatch. Pick premium (most capable), mid (balanced) or low (fastest); the platform maps the tier to a concrete provider model. A persisted concrete model id is forwarded verbatim.
examples: premium — hardest stages (planning, implementation).
mid — balanced default for routine stages.
low — cheap/fast auxiliary stages.

pipelineBuilderLlmTools.summary: Tools the LLM is allowed to call during this step. Both Claude Code built-ins (Read/Edit/Bash/…) and MCP tools (mcp__valaris__*) live here. Enforced server-side by the MCP allowlist middleware.
examples: e.g. a code-writing step: Read, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, mcp__valaris__create_note.
e.g. a read-only review step: Read, Grep, mcp__valaris__get_card — no Edit/Bash.
e.g. a backlog-planning step: mcp__valaris__* only — no filesystem access.

callouts.text: Drop a tool here, and the runner sends a fresh --mcp-config to the CLI with that tool removed from VALARIS_MCP_ALLOWLIST. The LLM cannot see or call it.

pipelineBuilderLlmApprovalEnabled.summary: When on, the runner stops after the LLM step and waits for a human verdict before continuing the lifecycle. A brake on expensive or high-impact steps so a person reviews before the pipeline proceeds.
examples: Leave off for a step that is itself meant to be the authority (e.g. a step that emits the review verdict).
Turn on for first-touch human gating of a costly code-writing step during an incident drill.

pipelineApplyLabel.summary: Adds a label to the current card. Labels are free-form strings used by discover filters and branch expressions downstream, so this is the primary way one step signals state to another. Non-terminal — the walk continues to the next step.
examples: Add `planned` so a later discover step keyed on require_label can pick the card up.
Add `needs-rework` to route a card back into a fix loop.
Adding an existing label is a no-op; it never errors.

pipelineRemoveLabel.summary: Removes a label from the current card. The mirror of apply_label — used to clear a state flag so the card stops matching a label-keyed discover filter or branch case.
examples: Remove `needs-rework` once a fix lands so the card leaves the rework loop.
Removing a label the card doesn't have is a no-op; it never errors.

pipelineWakeRoleRoles.summary: Comma-separated list of role names to wake. Waking a role nudges the scheduler to re-evaluate it on the next tick so it can pick up work this step just made eligible — without waiting for its normal poll interval.
examples: After labeling a card `planned`, wake the role whose discover filter requires that label.
Names are matched against the roles defined in this pipeline config; an unknown name is silently ignored.
Multiple roles: `builder, reviewer`.

callouts.text: Waking only schedules a re-check — it never forces a role to run if its discover filter finds no claimable work.

pipelineEnqueueForMerge.summary: Places the card's PR onto the workspace merge queue instead of merging immediately. The queue serializes integration so parallel cards merge one at a time against an up-to-date base. Terminal — ends this walk; the queue worker drives the merge later.
examples: strategy: the merge method the queue should use when its turn comes (e.g. `squash`).
Use when the workspace runs multiple cards in parallel and needs conflict-safe serial integration.
Leave strategy blank to inherit the workspace default.

pipelineMergePrStrategy.summary: Merges the card's open PR right now using the chosen Git strategy. Direct merge (no queue) — appropriate for serial pipelines where only one card integrates at a time.

rows.label: merge
rows.value: Standard merge commit; preserves every commit on the branch.

rows.label: squash
rows.value: Collapses all branch commits into one before merging.

rows.label: rebase
rows.value: Replays branch commits onto the base with no merge commit.

pipelineEnableAutoMergeStrategy.summary: Turns on GitHub's auto-merge for the card's PR with the chosen strategy. The PR then merges itself once required checks and reviews pass — the runner does not block waiting. Non-terminal.

rows.label: merge
rows.value: Merge commit when checks pass.

rows.label: squash
rows.value: Squash to a single commit when checks pass.

rows.label: rebase
rows.value: Rebase onto base when checks pass.

callouts.text: Requires auto-merge to be enabled on the repo. If checks never pass, the PR simply stays open.

pipelineMoveCardToColumnType.summary: Moves the card to the first column of the given type. Columns are addressed by their type (not name) so the same step works across boards with differently-named columns. Terminal — ends this walk.

rows.label: backlog
rows.value: Not yet started / queued.

rows.label: active
rows.value: In progress.

rows.label: review
rows.value: Awaiting review or verification.

rows.label: done
rows.value: Completed.

rows.label: blocked
rows.value: Stalled on a dependency or external factor.

callouts.text: Moving to `done` may be gated by the workspace done-merge policy (a card without a merged PR can be refused).

pipelineShipToColumnType.summary: Marks the card shipped and moves it to the chosen column type. Like move_card but carries explicit ship semantics — typically the final terminal step after a PR is merged. Addressed by column type, not name.

rows.label: done
rows.value: Most common ship target.

rows.label: review
rows.value: Ship into a verification lane before fully closing.

rows.label: backlog / active / blocked
rows.value: Available for non-standard lifecycles.

pipelineCreateFixCardsToColumnType.summary: Which column the new fix cards land in. Default 'active' lets an implementer pick them up directly without planning.

pipelineCreateFixCardsLabels.summary: Fixed label stamp applied to every created fix card. 'direct-implement' routes small fixes past the planner straight to the implementer.

pipelineCreateFixCardsPriority.summary: Priority stamped on every created fix card. 'urgent' surfaces audit-found regressions ahead of routine backlog.

pipelineBranchExpression.summary: An expression evaluated against the run context (the prior step's decision, card fields, labels). Its result is matched against the keys in `cases` to choose the next step. This is how a pipeline forks on a decision or condition.
examples: Reference the upstream decision token, e.g. an expression that yields `approve` or `request_changes`.
The evaluated value is looked up in `cases`; the matching branch's step runs next.
If no case matches, the walk falls through (see the cases field for the default).

pipelineBranchCases.summary: A JSON object mapping each possible value of `expression` to the step that should run for it. Defines the fork's edges — one entry per outcome you want to handle.

callouts.text: Values are step references in this pipeline. A `default` key (if present) catches any unmatched expression result.

pipelineClaimExecutionAction.summary: A label recorded on the execution row this claim opens. It tags what the actor is about to do so execution-history context and dashboards can group runs by action. Free-form string.
examples: A token like `implement` or `review` describing the work this claim represents.
Surfaces in the execution_history context source so later steps can see what prior runs did.
Purely descriptive — it does not change runner behavior.

pipelineCreateNoteKind.summary: The note-registry key the new note is filed under (e.g. plan, review_verdict, rework_brief). Downstream context sources and discover filters select notes by kind, so this routes the note to whoever consumes it.
examples: Use a kind a downstream step reads, e.g. a card_notes context source filtered to that kind.
Some kinds are immutable once written (e.g. review verdicts).
Free-form, but matching an existing convention keeps consumers wired up.

pipelineCreateNoteFromLlmOutput.summary: When on, the note body is filled from the preceding LLM step's output instead of a static template. Use it to persist what the model produced (a plan, a summary, a verdict) as a durable card note.

callouts.text: Requires an LLM step earlier in the walk whose output is available in context; otherwise the note body is empty.

pipelineCreatePrTitleFrom.summary: Which source the PR title is drawn from. Reserved for future templating — the runner currently uses a fixed default (the card title) and ignores this field. Set it now to document intent.
examples: Future: select a context channel (e.g. the card title or an LLM-produced summary).
Today: leave blank; the runner uses the card title.

pipelineCreatePrBodyFrom.summary: Which source the PR body is drawn from. Reserved for future templating — the runner currently uses fixed defaults (the LLM result summary/findings) and ignores this field.
examples: Future: select which output channel fills the body.
Today: leave blank; the runner composes a default body.

pipelineDiscoverColumnType.summary: Restricts discovery to cards sitting in a column of this type. Used with the column_scan strategy to pull work from one lane. Matches by column type, not name, so it is board-agnostic.
examples: `backlog` to claim fresh queued work; `review` to pick up cards awaiting verification.
Leave blank when the strategy already scopes the search (e.g. unassigned_or_rework scans the whole board).

pipelineDiscoverColumnTypeExclude.summary: Excludes cards in a column of this type from discovery, even if they otherwise match. A guard rail to keep a step from re-picking cards in a terminal or in-flight lane.
examples: Exclude `done` so a scanner never re-processes finished cards.
Exclude `blocked` to skip cards stalled on dependencies.

pipelineDiscoverPreconditions.summary: Named gates that must all hold before a found card is eligible. Each tag maps to a server-side check (e.g. an open PR exists, no unresolved blockers). A card failing any precondition is skipped.
examples: Require an open PR before a step that posts a review.
Require dependencies satisfied before a step that ships the card.
Add multiple tags — all must pass (AND).

callouts.text: Precondition names are a closed server-side set; an unknown name is ignored by the scheduler.

pipelineDiscoverFilters.summary: A JSON object of extra match constraints layered on top of strategy and column scope — narrow discovery by labels, pipeline role, card type, priority, and more. All keys must match (AND).

callouts.text: require_pipeline_role / skip_if_pipeline_role key on the claim step's pipeline_role — the canonical way roles avoid stealing each other's cards.

pipelineGitSetupAction.summary: What this step does to the working tree before the actor runs. Prepares Git so a code-writing or review step starts from the right branch.

rows.label: create_branch
rows.value: Cut a fresh branch from base_ref for new work.

rows.label: checkout_pr_branch
rows.value: Check out the card's existing PR branch (e.g. to add rework commits).

rows.label: none
rows.value: Leave the working tree as-is — for steps that don't touch code.

pipelineGitSetupBranchPrefix.summary: Prefix prepended to the auto-generated branch name when action is create_branch. Lets you namespace branches per role or workflow. The runner appends a card-derived slug after the prefix.
examples: `feat/` produces branches like `feat/<card-slug>`.
`rework/` to distinguish rework branches in the repo.
Leave blank for the runner default.

pipelineGitSetupBaseRef.summary: Which ref a newly created branch forks from. Determines whether work integrates against mainline or a shared integration branch used to serialize parallel cards.

rows.label: default_branch
rows.value: Branch from the repo's default branch (e.g. main).

rows.label: integration_branch
rows.value: Branch from the workspace integration branch so parallel cards stack safely before final merge.

pipelineGitSetupCreatePr.summary: When on, open a PR immediately after creating the branch (before the actor has produced commits). Use when the rest of the pipeline expects an open PR to exist — e.g. a step gated on a PR being present.

callouts.text: Most flows create the PR later via a dedicated create_pr step instead; enable this only when an early PR is required.

pipelineGitSetupForcePushOnRework.summary: When on, a rework pass force-pushes over the existing branch instead of layering new commits. Keeps the PR history clean on retry, at the cost of overwriting the prior pushed state.

callouts.text: Force-push rewrites remote history on the branch. Only safe on a single-actor feature branch the pipeline owns.

pipelineMcpCallTool.summary: The MCP tool to invoke directly as a pipeline step — no LLM involved. The runner calls the tool with the args below and continues. Use for deterministic side effects you don't want a model deciding on.
examples: A workspace tool name, e.g. mcp__valaris__create_card or mcp__valaris__update_card.
Runs server-side under the same allowlist the LLM steps obey.
Pairs with the args field below for the call payload.

pipelineMcpCallArgs.summary: The JSON argument object passed to the tool named above. Keys and shape are whatever that tool expects — the runner forwards the object verbatim.

pipelinePostPrReviewDecision.summary: The review verdict this step posts to the card's PR. Drives whether the PR is approved, sent back for changes, or just commented on. Often paired with an upstream branch step that selected the decision.

rows.label: approve
rows.value: Posts an approving review.

rows.label: request_changes
rows.value: Posts a changes-requested review (blocks merge on GitHub).

rows.label: comment
rows.value: Posts a non-blocking comment review.

pipelinePostPrReviewBodyFrom.summary: Which output channel supplies the review body text. Reserved for future templating — the runner currently uses fixed defaults (the upstream LLM summary/findings) and ignores this field.
examples: Future: pick the findings or summary channel from a prior LLM step.
Today: leave blank; the runner composes the body from defaults.

rows.label: github
rows.value: Posts a formal GitHub PR review (approve/request_changes carry their GitHub semantics).

rows.label: comment
rows.value: Posts as a plain comment instead of a formal review.

pipelineSensorName.summary: Selects which built-in sensor (a deterministic, non-LLM check) runs at this step. The sensor inspects external state and emits a pass/fail decision the on_pass / on_fail edges branch on.
examples: A registered sensor name, e.g. one that checks CI status or whether a PR is mergeable.
The sensor's config object below tunes what it checks.
Sensors are a closed server/runner-side set; an unknown name fails the step.

pipelineSensorOnPass.summary: The step to run next when the sensor returns pass. This is the success edge of the sensor's fork.
examples: Point a CI-status sensor's pass edge at a merge step.
References a step in this pipeline by name.

pipelineSensorOnFail.summary: The step to run next when the sensor returns fail. This is the failure edge of the sensor's fork.
examples: Point a CI-status sensor's fail edge at a rework or notify step.
References a step in this pipeline by name.

pipelineSensorConfig.summary: JSON configuration passed to the selected sensor. Shape depends entirely on the sensor — it tunes thresholds, target checks, or timeouts. The runner forwards it verbatim.

pipelineEnd.summary: A no-op terminal step. It does nothing except stop the walk. Use it to give a non-terminal step (like apply_label) an explicit place to end a branch instead of relying on terminal-by-default behavior.
examples: End a failure branch after labeling a card, when no further action is wanted.
Make a branch case's terminus explicit and readable.

pipelineContextSourceKind.summary: The type of backend-rendered context block to inject into this step's LLM call. Each kind is fetched server-side at assignment time and exposed to the prompt under its alias. The prompt must reference the alias for the block to reach the model.

rows.label: Card notes
rows.value: Notes on the worked card; filter by note kind.

rows.label: Board definition
rows.value: The board's north-star / pillars / principles document.

rows.label: Pinned notes
rows.value: Notes pinned at board or workspace level.

rows.label: Sibling cards
rows.value: Other cards on the board; filter by column/label/priority.

rows.label: Board snapshot
rows.value: Full board grouped by column.

rows.label: Review history
rows.value: Past verdicts recorded on this card.

rows.label: Dependency health
rows.value: Board dependency-graph faults (cycles, conflicts, dangling edges).

rows.label: Linked cards
rows.value: This card's own depends-on / blocks edges, with done-state.

rows.label: Execution history
rows.value: Prior agent runs on this card (action, role, model, outcome).

rows.label: Card activity
rows.value: The card's move / participant / note timeline.

rows.label: Pipeline expectations
rows.value: The pipeline config the actor runs under — output shape, decision vocabulary, allowed tools.

callouts.text: Declaring a source does nothing until the prompt references its alias. The Prompts page shows green/amber chips for this.

pipelineContextSourceFilter.summary: Per-kind narrowing for the selected context source — only some kinds expose one. It scopes what the block contains so the prompt isn't flooded with irrelevant context.
examples: Card notes: limit to one note kind (e.g. only review verdicts).
Sibling cards: filter by column type, label, priority, or a cap.
Kinds without a filter (e.g. board definition) show nothing here.

pipelineContextSourceAs.summary: The alias this source is exposed under inside the prompt. The prompt references it as {{ index .ContextSources "alias" }}. Defaults to the kind name when blank.
examples: Set `verdicts` to reference review history as {{ index .ContextSources "verdicts" }}.
Use distinct aliases when declaring two sources of the same kind.
Leave blank to use the kind name as the alias.

cardTypeTask.summary: Generic unit of work. Default choice when the other types don't fit. Implementer treats it like a feature unless labels steer otherwise.

cardTypeBug.summary: Defect to diagnose and fix. Implementer is expected to reproduce the issue, write a failing test, then ship the fix. Reviewer should check for regression coverage.

cardTypeFeature.summary: New capability to build. Implementer starts from requirements, reviewer checks behavior matches the spec, and the documentation owner records user-facing changes.

cardTypeIssue.summary: User-reported problem or question that may or may not require code changes. Often gets triaged into a bug or feature before implementation begins.

roleImplementer.summary: Primary-owner role that writes code. Claims cards, cuts a branch, runs the implement prompt, commits, and opens a PR.
examples: Typically the highest-spend role — pair with the strongest model (Opus).
Uses `writes_code` post-processing; on_failure routes to a rework column.

roleReviewer.summary: Collaborator role that inspects an open PR and emits an approve/request_changes decision. Never pushes commits.
examples: Uses `produces_decision` post-processing with structured output.
Directive compliance is critical — use Opus or enable inject_directives.

roleDocumentator.summary: Collaborator role that records what shipped. Reads merged diffs and produces a card note explaining the change for downstream runners and humans.
examples: Uses `produces_note` post-processing.
Runs after the card hits the done column — no git write access needed.

rolePlanner.summary: Collaborator or primary-owner role that mutates the backlog — splits oversized cards, orders a sprint, or re-prioritizes. Reads context only; no code writes.
examples: Uses `mutates_backlog` post-processing.
git.action is typically `none`.

roleReworkMediator.summary: Collaborator role that sits between a reviewer's request_changes verdict and the implementer's rework pass. Reads the verdict note and produces a rework_brief note distilling what to change and why.
examples: Uses `produces_note` post-processing; never pushes commits.
Discovers cards in `active` carrying a review_verdict note; skips cards already mediated.

promptStructuredOutput.summary: Schema that constrains the LLM's response to a machine-parseable shape. Required when post_process_kind expects structured data (e.g., reviewer's approve/request_changes decision).
examples: Reviewer: { decision: 'approve' | 'request_changes', reasoning: string }.
Planner: array of card-shaped objects to create or update.
Leave empty for free-form text stages (documentation owner, researcher).

status.summary: What the runner did on this tick. Not every status means something went wrong — skipped, in particular, is usually a healthy outcome.

rows.label: completed
rows.value: Stage ran end-to-end and returned cleanly.

rows.label: failed
rows.value: Stage errored before producing a result. error_message holds the reason.

rows.label: running
rows.value: Stage is in flight right now. Cost and tokens update when it finishes.

rows.label: started
rows.value: Claim succeeded; the LLM call has not yet returned.

rows.label: aborted
rows.value: Stage was killed mid-run — usually a timeout, budget cutoff, or operator intervention.

rows.label: skipped
rows.value: Runner polled, found a card, realized no prompt was authored for this (role, stage). It moved on instead of hallucinating.

callouts.text: Skipped is the single most-misread status on this panel. The runner did its job correctly — it didn't crash, it didn't fake an answer, it just had nothing to say. Author a prompt and the next tick will run.
A started that never transitions to completed or failed is the one to worry about. That's a runner that died mid-execution; check the runner's heartbeat.

role.summary: Team role the runner claimed the card under — a membership tag like hero or helper, or a custom role from your pipeline. Distinct from stage: one role typically drives several stages in sequence.
examples: hero: the exclusive owner of the card end-to-end.
helper: coexists with a hero — reviewers, documentation owners, researchers.
Custom role names come from your team's pipeline config. They are not validated against a fixed list.

stage.summary: Prompt slot the runner executed — the token that selects which prompt config to render. Role is who the runner claimed as; stage is what it just did.

rows.label: Resolved by
rows.value: (workspace, team, team_role, stage)

rows.label: Common stages
rows.value: implement, review, document, plan, research

rows.label: Custom stages
rows.value: Any string — but there must be a matching prompt config or the run skips.

callouts.text: One role can drive several stages on one card. An implementer role typically runs claim, implement, and ship across multiple ticks.

cardsAffected.summary: Cards this execution mutated — moved columns, added participants, edited description, attached notes. The claimed card is always included; custom decomposers and bulk-movers can touch several.
examples: Implementer run: one card (the claimed one).
Planner run: one card — its findings become a plan note on the claimed card.
Reviewer run: one — the card whose PR was reviewed.

toolInvocations.summary: Every MCP or coding-agent tool call the LLM made during this execution, in the order they ran. Useful for debugging why a stage took so long, cost so much, or produced an unexpected output.
examples: Read and Grep calls show what context the runner pulled before writing.
Bash calls reveal the shape of the work (build, test, git push).
A very long list on a supposedly simple stage is a hint the prompt is over-scoped.

callouts.text: Empty list on a completed run means the LLM produced output without calling any tools — typical for review stages that only emit a decision.

shipWarnings.summary: Non-fatal issues the ship stage ran into. The PR still merged and the card still moved, but something adjacent didn't go cleanly.
examples: auto-merge arming failed — the branch has no protection rules yet.
label not applied — GitHub returned 403 for the token's scope.
The card still shipped; these warnings are FYI, not a rollback signal.

callouts.text: Ship warnings batch together. One repo without branch protection can surface several warnings on every ship until protection is configured.

parentExecution.summary: This execution was forked from an earlier one — either a retry of a failed run or the next stage in a multi-stage pipeline chain on the same card.

rows.label: Retry
rows.value: Parent failed; the runner was eligible again next tick and re-claimed.

rows.label: Pipeline chain
rows.value: Parent completed a stage (e.g. implement) that hands off to the next stage (e.g. ship) on the same card.

rows.label: What to click
rows.value: The short hash opens the parent execution's detail page.

callouts.text: Parent IDs are UUIDs — the eight-character prefix is the shortest unique form that's still copy-pasteable. The full ID is in the parent's detail URL.

usage.summary: Cumulative USD this runner has spent in the current period. The bar tints amber past 80% and red once the budget is exceeded.

rows.label: spent_usd
rows.value: Sum of cost_usd across executions this period.

rows.label: budget_usd
rows.value: Per-runner cap. Blank means no cap — the runner will never stop on budget alone.

rows.label: remaining_usd
rows.value: budget_usd minus spent_usd. Negative values are allowed when a run overshoots.

callouts.text: Pricing comes from workspace_config.model_pricing. If that map is empty or stale, cost_usd reads zero and this panel will look idle even under heavy use.

periodReset.summary: Spend accumulates until the period rolls over. Rollover zeros the counter and unblocks polling — no manual reset needed once the new period begins.
examples: Mid-period spikes persist until rollover. Manual override means clearing the counter in workspace settings.
A run that started before rollover finishes normally — rollover only affects new claims.

exceeded.summary: Budget exceeded means new claims refuse. Runners keep heartbeating and draining in-flight work, but they stop picking up fresh cards until the next period or a bumped budget.

rows.label: Trigger
rows.value: spent_usd >= budget_usd on claim attempt.

rows.label: Effect
rows.value: Claim returns no-work; executions already running finish normally.

rows.label: Recovery
rows.value: Raise budget_usd or wait for the period rollover — either unblocks the next tick.

callouts.text: Setting a budget of $0 does what you'd expect: the runner refuses every claim from tick one. Ask us how we know.

alerts.summary: Threshold alerts notify when a metric crosses a line. They are observational — a firing alert does not stop the runner. Only the budget cap itself enforces.

rows.label: Alert
rows.value: Fires once per crossing. Surfaces in channels and the observer panel.

rows.label: Enforcement
rows.value: Separate knob — budget_usd on the runner. Only this refuses claims.

rows.label: Per-period rate caps
rows.value: Tracked in-memory per runner instance.

callouts.text: The per-minute rate limiter lives in process memory. Cloud Run scales to N instances, so the effective cap is N × limit. Fine for dev traffic; redesign before relying on it for real abuse protection.

rolesTabs.summary: Tabs are pipeline-driven — the list of roles here mirrors the roles declared in your pipeline config. Add a role to a stage in the Pipeline Builder and it shows up here on the next reload.

rows.label: Source
rows.value: pipeline_config.stages[*].role — deduplicated

rows.label: Order
rows.value: Insertion order in the pipeline, not alphabetical

rows.label: All
rows.value: Shows every stage across every role

callouts.text: A role that exists only on an override (no pipeline stage) will NOT appear as a tab. Wire it into the pipeline first.
Platform-shipped roles and operator-authored custom roles are rendered identically. Custom roles are not second-class here.

stageList.summary: Each row is a (role, stage) pair the pipeline can execute. The badge on the right states which layer the runner will end up using at run time.

rows.label: Default
rows.value: Platform-shipped prompt or backend-synthesized placeholder — no override authored

rows.label: Custom vN
rows.value: Operator-authored override; N is the save version, incremented on every update

callouts.text: Synthesized placeholders are rendered from a minimal template when the (role, stage) pair is not in the platform registry. They are still tagged Default — creating an override replaces them cleanly.

The runner always prefers the backend-assembled resolved_content over the raw content you edit here — the post-process imperative stays spliced in so stages like produces_note still call create_note after you save.

sections.title: Default
sections.summary: Registry default (21 hand-written stages) or synthesized placeholder for anything custom.

callouts.text: Safe to ship as-is — the platform registry is exercised by every smoke test.

sections.title: Custom vN
sections.summary: Your override is active. Reset to Default deletes the row and falls back to the registry/synthesized content.

callouts.text: Renaming the stage string in the Pipeline Builder orphans this override — the lookup key is (role, stage), not a foreign key.

templateVariables.summary: Variables Go `text/template` substitutes at render time. Click a chip to append `{{.Variable}}` to the editor. Undefined variables render as empty strings — typos fail silently, so copy the chip rather than typing from memory.

rows.label: {{.WorkspaceSlug}}
rows.value: Slug of the workspace the runner is operating in

rows.label: {{.BoardID}}
rows.value: UUID of the board the card lives on

rows.label: {{.CardID}}
rows.value: UUID of the card being worked — feed this to mcp__valaris__get_card

rows.label: {{.Title}}
rows.value: Card title, verbatim (e.g., "Add OIDC login to /auth")

rows.label: {{.ExecutionID}}
rows.value: UUID of this execution row — used by log_execution_update

rows.label: {{.ProjectDirectives}}
rows.value: Board definition + pinned notes; populated only when inject_directives: true on the stage

rows.label: {{.ReviewHistory}}
rows.value: Prior verdict notes pre-fetched by the runner; populated only on stages that opt in (e.g. a rework-mediation stage)

rows.label: {{.ActionPlan}}
rows.value: An upstream stage's structured plan, threaded forward; populated only on stages that opt in (e.g. a rework-implement stage)

callouts.text: Go template syntax — the leading dot is required. `{{.CardID}}` works; `{{CardID}}` does not.
Stage-specific variables (e.g. ReviewHistory, ActionPlan) are only populated on the stages that opt into them. Referencing one from a stage that doesn't provide it renders an empty string — silently.

The code-controlled context augmentation rule is why these variables exist: the platform fetches mandatory context and injects it under labelled sections, rather than asking the LLM to fetch it via tools.

examples: e.g. a code-writing stage: {{.CardID}}, {{.Title}}, {{.ProjectDirectives}}.
e.g. a rework-implement stage: add {{.ActionPlan}} to carry the upstream plan through.
e.g. a mediation stage: add {{.ReviewHistory}} to see prior findings verbatim.

contextSources.summary: Backend-rendered context blocks declared on this stage's pipeline config. Each declared source is fetched server-side and exposed to the prompt under its alias. Unlike template variables (the {{.Var}} form), these only reach the LLM when the prompt references them via the index form — click a chip to insert it correctly.

rows.label: Green chip
rows.value: Declared AND referenced in the prompt body — its rendered context reaches the LLM

rows.label: Amber chip
rows.value: Declared on the stage but not yet referenced — its rendered context is silently dropped

rows.label: Syntax
rows.value: {{ index .ContextSources "alias" }} — quotes and the index keyword are mandatory

rows.label: Alias
rows.value: The source's `as` value, falling back to its `kind` — set in the Pipeline Builder, not here

callouts.text: Wiring fails silently in BOTH directions: a declared source you never reference renders to nothing (amber chip + inline warning), and an alias you reference but never declare renders an empty string. Copy the chip rather than typing the alias by hand.
Sources are assembled at /next-assignment and shipped in the assignment bundle — code-controlled context the platform fetches server-side, never LLM-fetched at run time.

Two kinds bridge to the prompt through legacy struct fields instead of the index form: board_definition via {{.ProjectDirectives}} and review_history via {{.ReviewHistory}}. Declaring those and using the legacy field is correct wiring — they won't warn.

editor.summary: Plain textarea. No syntax highlighting, no variable autocomplete, no preview, no lint. Most authors use the MCP tool create_prompt_config from their IDE for anything non-trivial — same result, proper editor.

callouts.text: The editor is a textarea because the prompt-authoring UX is explicitly on the backlog. Treating it like one (edit elsewhere, paste here) is the path of least surprise.

Nothing here validates your Go template — a missing closing brace saves cleanly and fails at the runner when the next execution tries to render it. Exercise the stage on a throwaway card after a substantive edit.

The post-process imperative is spliced in by the backend on save — you do not need to write "Call create_note(...)" by hand; pick the post_process_kind on the pipeline stage and the imperative lands in resolved_content.

saveButton.summary: Writes an AgentPromptConfig row scoped to (workspace, team, role, stage, slug). Idempotent — saving twice with the same content bumps the version without creating duplicates.

callouts.text: The backend re-splices the post-process imperative on every save. The resolved_content the runner sees is always current with the stage's post_process_kind.
Save does not validate template syntax. An unbalanced `{{` lands in the DB; the runner fails on next render.

resetButton.summary: Deletes your override and falls back to the platform default (or synthesized placeholder for custom roles). Not undoable — the content is gone from the DB.

callouts.text: There is no recycle bin. Export the override first if there's any chance you want it back.
Reset is per-stage. Other overrides on other stages of the same role stay intact.

createNewStage.summary: Authors a prompt for a (role, stage) pair that does not yet appear in the list — typically because a custom stage was added to the pipeline without reloading, or the role is declared only in the override layer.

rows.label: Role
rows.value: Free-form string — must match pipeline_config.stages[*].role for the runner to pick it up

rows.label: Stage
rows.value: Lowercase token — must match the stage's llm.stage field

rows.label: Content
rows.value: Go template source; the same variables and rules as the main editor

callouts.text: An override with no matching pipeline stage is legal but useless — the runner looks up prompts by (role, stage) declared in the pipeline, not by what you authored here.
Deep-linkable: the Awaiting Prompt chip on a card appends ?role=X&stage=Y and opens this dialog pre-filled.

deepLinkHint.summary: This field accepts the exact lowercase token from your pipeline config's llm.stage. The runner looks up prompts by (role, stage) — a typo here silently produces an override the runner never reads.
examples: `security_review` matches `llm.stage: security_review`.
`Security Review` does not match — case and spacing are significant.
Deep links from Awaiting Prompt chips prefill this field verbatim.

wiredBadge.summary: This (role, stage) pair is reachable from the live pipeline config — at least one stage will look this prompt up by its (role, stage) key and execute it. Hover the badge itself to see exactly which stage(s).

callouts.text: Wired means executable on this workspace. An edit you save here takes effect on the next execution of that stage.
Wiring is computed from the pipeline config, not from whether an override exists. A Default (no override) prompt can be wired, and a Custom override can be orphaned.

orphanBadge.summary: No pipeline stage references this (role, stage) pair, so the runner never looks it up — nothing here executes. Authoring or editing it is harmless but inert until a stage in the Pipeline Builder declares the matching role + llm.stage.

callouts.text: Common cause: the stage was renamed in the Pipeline Builder, or the role was removed from the pipeline. The lookup key is (role, stage) — it is not a foreign key, so renames orphan silently.
To wire it: add a stage to the pipeline whose role and llm.stage match this row exactly (case- and spacing-sensitive).

createOverride.summary: Forks the active default into an editable copy scoped to this workspace. Until you do this, the runner uses the platform default (or a synthesized placeholder for a custom role) shown above — read-only.

callouts.text: An override only changes behavior on THIS workspace. The platform default and every other workspace are untouched.
Reset to Default later deletes the override and falls back to the same content shown here. Nothing is lost from the platform default by overriding it.

deletion.summary: The runner is about to delete a card, note, or resource the platform considers non-trivially recoverable. Base risk score 60; bumps to 80 once more than one item is in scope, and another +10 when the scope is board-wide.

rows.value: item_count > 1 or card_ids length > 1
board_level: true (cleanup spanning a whole board)

callouts.text: Deletes are not undos — the row is gone once the action fires. If you're unsure, reject and have the runner archive instead.

bulk_change.summary: Mutation touches many records in one shot (priority sweep, label retag, participant churn). Base score 40; each block of 10 items adds 10, capped at +40.

rows.label: +10 per 10 items
rows.value: capped at +40 (i.e. 40 items or more)

callouts.text: The risk score cares about breadth, not direction — a well-targeted edit on 200 cards scores the same as a sloppy one.

deployment.summary: Runner is about to push to an environment (staging, production, preview). Base 70; production adds another 20, staging subtracts 20.

rows.value: environment: production
environment: staging

callouts.text: Preview environments default to the base score — if your preview infra touches shared data, treat it like production.

schema_change.summary: Migration, index rebuild, column rename, constraint flip. Base 80 — the highest baseline the heuristic hands out. Destructive migrations (drop column/table) add another 10.

rows.value: destructive: true (drop column, drop table, drop constraint)

callouts.text: Rolling-update safety still applies — reject here if the new schema isn't backwards-compatible with the currently-running code.

permission_change.summary: Role or membership edit (add a member, change a role, rotate an API key's scope). Base 50; promotions to admin or owner add a hefty 30.

rows.value: role: admin or owner (privilege escalation)

callouts.text: Demotions and removals score the same as additions — the heuristic doesn't read direction, only blast radius.

external_action.summary: Runner is calling out to a system the platform doesn't control (GitHub API, webhook, third-party integration). Base 30 — the lowest baseline. A push or PR merge against `main`, `master`, or `production` adds 20.

rows.value: branch in [main, master, production]

callouts.text: The score is low by default because most external actions (fetch, comment, status check) are idempotent. The branch bump exists because merges into protected branches aren't.

skill_publication.summary: A loop agent proposed publishing a new skill version. Base 60 — a published skill changes what every future agent session on this workspace is taught, so it can never auto-approve.
