callouts.text: Approving publishes the proposed version as the skill’s latest; rejecting keeps the currently published version in place.

riskScore.summary: A 0–100 category-weighted heuristic the backend computes at request time. It is not a machine-learning model — there is no training loop and no feedback from your past decisions.

rows.value: Auto-approved (threshold is 30; tune AUTO_APPROVE_THRESHOLD in code).
Low — likely safe; still requires a human tick.
Medium — inspect the payload before approving.
High — read the action_description, then read it again.

callouts.text: The score is a category-weighted heuristic in backend/app/services/approvals/risk.py. It will not learn from your past decisions. Tune it in code if it consistently under- or over-alerts.
Low-score approvals that cross the auto-approve threshold skip this queue entirely — they only show up in history, already decided.

expiry.summary: Pending approvals expire 24 hours after creation. Expired approvals flip to `expired` status and the runner treats them as a rejection — it will not resume the stage.

callouts.text: The 24-hour default is not configurable per-request today. If you need a different window, change expires_at on the ApprovalService.create path.
Expiring is terminal: the runner that requested the approval has usually moved on by the time you see the stale row. Re-triggering the work means re-running the pipeline stage.

approve.summary: Marks the approval resolved and wakes the waiting runner via WebSocket. The runner resumes through the `implement_after_approval` path and continues the stage.

callouts.text: Approvals are append-once — after you approve, the same approval cannot be edited or revoked. The runner fires on the decision event.

reject.summary: Terminal. Rejecting abandons the runner's current action; it will not retry this approval. Provide a reason so the next operator — or the runner itself — understands why.

callouts.text: Rejection does not undo anything the runner did before requesting the gate — it only blocks the next step. If partial work already landed, clean it up out-of-band.
A rejected approval with the same (agent, card, action) signature can reappear if the runner re-requests on its next tick. The reason field persists; the runner's prompt should be reading it back.

prefix.summary: First eight characters of the key. Displayed so you can match a key in the list against the one a runner is using (via execution logs or the MCP tracking record) without exposing the secret material.
examples: `vlr_ab12cd34` — everything after the 8th character stays hidden.
The runner execution tracker discovers which agent a tool call came from by looking up this prefix.

kanban.summary: The main board view. Columns, cards, drag-and-drop, live runner activity.

definitions.summary: Structured context the board ships to every runner prompt — mission, stack, conventions, non-goals. Edit here once; every LLM stage picks it up via directive injection.

resources.summary: Files and links scoped to this board. GCS-backed with signed URLs; runners can read them via the MCP resource tools.

notes.summary: Board-scoped notes — decisions, learnings, pinned context. Notes tagged `directive` are prepended to prompts when the stage has inject_directives enabled.

history.summary: Chronological activity log for this board — card moves, runner executions, note edits. The read-only audit trail when something looks wrong.

timeline.summary: A video-like replay of this board's full history — play, pause, scrub through every move, and click a card for its dwell-per-column and who-held-it analytics. Read-only.

git.summary: Git repositories linked to this board. Runners with git.action != none check these out; a board with zero repos means implementer stages will skip.

alerts.summary: Board-level alert thresholds — health score, stale/overdue counts, cost. Breached thresholds surface on the dashboard and in channels.

languageSwitcher.summary: Selects the UI language: English, Spanish, or Brazilian Portuguese. Preference persists in localStorage. Does not translate user-generated content — card titles, notes, and prompts stay in whatever language you wrote them.

themeSwitcher.summary: Picks the color theme. System follows your OS preference and flips with it; Light and Dark pin the choice.

rows.label: System
rows.value: Matches OS — flips live if you change OS appearance.

rows.label: Light
rows.value: Pinned light surfaces. Best on projectors and sun-bleached windows.

rows.label: Dark
rows.value: Pinned dark surfaces. The default most of us actually use.

connected.summary: Live WebSocket connection is healthy. The board, Observer, and runner overview update in real time.

connecting.summary: Reconnecting to the platform. Live updates are briefly paused; recent events will replay once the socket is back.

callouts.text: If this state persists past a few seconds, check your network — the client auto-retries with backoff.

disconnected.summary: No live WebSocket connection. The UI is running on its last-known state.

callouts.text: Live events are stale. Pages that rely on them (Kanban board, Runner overview) show their last-known state. HTTP-poll fallbacks on a few hooks may still be refreshing; most are not.
Reload the tab if the indicator doesn't return to green within a minute — the socket's retry ladder eventually gives up.

intro.summary: Firehose of platform events, live from the workspace event bus. Admin-only by deliberate choice. In-memory and ephemeral: the most recent 1000 events, nothing persisted, cleared on reload. Card/Runner/Execution/Approval show by default; the Other chip appears when the bus carries anything else.

pause.summary: Stops appending new events to the list. Already-visible rows stay; incoming events are dropped on the floor, not buffered. Resume to start tailing again.

clear.summary: Empties the event list. Useful when you're hunting a specific tick and the log has scrolled past it. Cannot be undone — events live on the server, but the panel doesn't re-fetch history.

namespaceFilter.summary: Narrows the stream to one or more event namespaces. Chips are additive — pick Card + Runner to see both, click All to drop every filter.

columnName.summary: Human-facing column label. Rename freely — pipeline behaviour keys off the column type, not the name.

callouts.text: Two columns named 'Review' and 'Peer Review' behave identically if they share column_type. The label is for humans; the type is for runners.

columnType.summary: Semantic label that pipeline stages target. Distinct from the column's display name.

rows.label: backlog
rows.value: Unclaimed work. Default hunting ground for discover strategies.

rows.label: active
rows.value: In-progress work; an implementer hero is expected to be attached.

rows.label: review
rows.value: Ready for a reviewer stage to inspect the open PR.

rows.label: done
rows.value: Shipped. Documentation-owner stages may still attach post-ship notes.

rows.label: blocked
rows.value: Circuit-breaker stop. The scheduler skips every card in this column.

callouts.text: Renaming the column changes its display label only. Changing the type reroutes pipeline behaviour for every card in it.
column_scan with an empty column_type never finds work. Ask us how we know.

cardCount.summary: How many cards currently live in this column. Updated in real time as cards move.

callouts.text: A column showing zero cards isn't broken — it's just waiting. Discover strategies target column_type, so an empty 'Review' column means nothing is ready for review yet.

doneGateEnforced.summary: This workspace requires cards to be merged (e.g. via a PR) before landing in this column. Cards without a mergeable change may sit here until that happens.

addCardButton.summary: Create a new card directly in this column. Title is required; other fields can be filled in later from the detail sheet.

callouts.text: Keyboard shortcut: press n anywhere on the board to open the dialog against the leftmost column.
Creating a card in a blocked or done column is allowed, but the scheduler will skip it there — move it to a backlog or active column when you actually want a runner to pick it up.

priorityChip.summary: Operator signal for ordering. Influences discover-strategy ordering and the visual left-edge stripe — it does not change how hard the LLM tries.

rows.label: low
rows.value: Bottom of the queue. Picked up when nothing urgent is sitting around.

rows.label: medium
rows.value: Default. No special treatment.

rows.label: high
rows.value: Bumped ahead of medium in position-sorted discover passes.

rows.label: urgent
rows.value: Top of the queue. Strongly bumped in position-sorted discover passes.

callouts.text: Setting priority to urgent does not make the LLM work faster. It just changes which card gets claimed first.

cardTypeChip.summary: What kind of work this card represents. Implementers branch behaviour off this; reviewers use it to pick a rubric.

rows.label: task
rows.value: Generic unit of work. Treated like a feature unless labels say otherwise.

rows.label: bug
rows.value: Defect to diagnose and fix. Implementer should reproduce, write a failing test, then fix.

rows.label: feature
rows.value: New capability. Implementer builds from requirements; reviewer checks behaviour matches the spec.

rows.label: issue
rows.value: User-reported problem or question. Often triaged into bug or feature before implementation.

callouts.text: The type is advisory context for the LLM, not a hard filter. A bug-typed card still routes through the same stages as a task unless your pipeline explicitly filters on card_type.

labels.summary: Free-form string tags. Used by filter UI, discover-strategy include/exclude filters, and post-action effects.
examples: `documented` — e.g. added by a doc-writing stage on success; pair with exclude_label on the discover filter to avoid redundant runs.
`needs-rework` — e.g. added by a review stage's request_changes branch to route the card back to a code-writing stage.
`external-blocker` — operator-authored; doesn't trigger any pipeline branch by default, but filters nicely in the filter bar.

callouts.text: Labels are case-sensitive strings. The platform will not protect you from a typo — `Needs-rework` and `needs-rework` are two different labels.

active.summary: A runner is executing a pipeline stage against this card right now. Click the icon to jump to the live execution detail.

callouts.text: The pulse animation is driven by the card's agent_presence flag, which the backend sets when an execution with status=started references the card.

eligible.summary: A runner could work this card — it has an agent participant attached but no execution is in flight.

callouts.text: Eligible is the steady state when a hero is assigned but the scheduler hasn't ticked yet, or when the runner is mid-poll between stages.

touched.summary: Last worked {{when}}. A runner has acted on this card before; no execution is in flight right now.

callouts.text: Touched is a historical marker, not a live status. A card can be touched and still stuck — check the stuck-reasons panel in the detail sheet.

suspended.summary: Suspended. A runner hit its budget ceiling mid-implementation and checkpointed the work-in-progress; the card is parked, not being worked right now.

callouts.text: The branch already holds the partial work. The implementer resumes from where it left off on its next pickup — the scheduler sheds any stale reservation so it can re-discover the card.

awaitingPrompt.summary: A runner attempted a pipeline stage that has no prompt authored, so the execution was skipped without running the LLM.

callouts.text: This badge reflects a real skipped execution in the card's history — it's not hypothetical. Author the missing prompt before the scheduler retries.

skippedExecution.summary: One or more executions against this card were skipped because the pipeline stage had no prompt authored. The LLM never ran.

callouts.text: Open the card's runner activity subtab to see which (role, stage) pairs are missing prompts, then author them from the prompt config page.

stateBlocked.summary: This card is waiting on one or more upstream cards. The scheduler will skip it for stages that gate on `all_dependencies_done` until every upstream lands in a done-typed column.

callouts.text: Open the card to see the full list of cards blocking it and the cards waiting on it.

stateUnblocked.summary: All upstream dependencies of this card are satisfied (every prerequisite has landed in a done-typed column). The card is eligible for pickup.

callouts.text: This state only renders for cards that originally had dependencies. Brand-new cards with no deps show no chip at all.

agentStatusBar.summary: Runners currently executing a pipeline stage against a card on this board. Each badge shows the stage token and the role in flight.

callouts.text: The stage token (implement, review, document, ...) is the prompt selector — it matches the (role, stage) pair the backend looked up to assemble the running prompt.

This bar polls executions every couple of minutes today; it does not yet live-update on every execution.started / .completed event. A badge may linger a few seconds after the runner actually finishes.

boardHealthBadge.summary: Composite health score (0–100) derived from stale, overdue, unassigned, and blocked card counts against board velocity. Green at 80+, amber at 50+, red below.

rows.label: Green (80–100)
rows.value: Board is moving. Stale and overdue counts are low relative to velocity.

rows.label: Amber (50–79)
rows.value: Some drag. A few stale or unassigned cards — worth a triage pass.

rows.label: Red (0–49)
rows.value: Stuck. Overdue and stale counts dominate, or velocity has cratered.

callouts.text: The score is computed on-demand by the backend health endpoint, not continuously streamed. Expect the number to lag card mutations by one refresh cycle.

dueDate.summary: Soft deadline shown on the card and used by some discover strategies to pull overdue cards forward.

callouts.text: Overdue cards render the date in red and count toward the board health score's overdue tally.
Due date is advisory. The pipeline does not sulk if you miss it — it keeps working the card on the next tick either way.

status.summary: Per-card status string (todo / in_progress / in_review / done / blocked). Distinct from the column's column_type, which is the primitive the scheduler actually reads.

callouts.text: Status is a human label the runner can set via update_card_status to advertise progress; column_type is the pipeline-DSL primitive that drives discover strategies.
A card with status=done sitting in a backlog column is still discoverable by stages scanning the backlog. The scheduler does not read status — move the card to a done-typed column to stop claims.

participantRole.summary: The role a user or runner holds on this card. One hero per card is the convention; helpers, viewers, and stakeholders can coexist freely.

rows.label: hero
rows.value: Primary executor. Exactly one per card — enforced in the claim service. Implementer-style stages claim as hero.

rows.label: helper
rows.value: Secondary contributor. Reviewers, documentation owners, and researchers typically claim as helpers so they don't fight the hero for ownership.

rows.label: viewer
rows.value: Read-only observer. Receives WS notifications for the card but does not claim or mutate.

rows.label: stakeholder
rows.value: Interested party (product, design). Same permissions as viewer today; the distinction is for human organization.

callouts.text: The one-hero rule is enforced in the claim service, not by a DB constraint. Two agents racing for the same card both succeed at the API layer; the losing claim gets 409 from the service-level SELECT FOR UPDATE.

blockedColumn.summary: The card sits in a column_type=blocked column, so every pipeline stage's discover pass skips it.

callouts.text: Moving the card to a non-blocked column is the only way to let runners discover it again. The scheduler does not peek past a blocked column.

needsAdvisor.summary: The stuck-loop detector saw the same review feedback repeated and parked the card with the needs-advisor label. Reviewer and coder agents skip it until the label is removed.

callouts.text: Unparking is manual by design: resolve whatever the loop kept tripping on, then remove the needs-advisor label to re-queue the card for agents.

noHero.summary: The card has no participant with role=hero, and the pipeline contains at least one stage that claims as hero.

callouts.text: Implementer-style stages claim as hero via discover.strategy=unassigned_or_rework. If the stage's filters (labels, git repo, column) reject the card, the card stays heroless.
If your pipeline uses only helper-style claims, this reason does not surface — we gate it on whether any stage actually claims as hero.

awaitingPrompt.summary: One or more (role, stage) pairs in the pipeline have no prompt authored, and a runner already tried them against this card and skipped.

callouts.text: A skipped execution is a real historical event — it appears in the card's execution history with status=skipped. Author the prompt, and the next tick runs it for real.

requestChanges.summary: The latest review note on this card parsed as request_changes. Until a rework commit lands and a fresh review approves, the card is gated.

callouts.text: Review decisions are parsed from note titles matching `Review: <role> — approve|request_changes`. A fresh approve-variant note unblocks the card.

recentFailures.summary: Two or more executions against this card failed in the last 24 hours. The scheduler's failure backoff throttles subsequent attempts.

callouts.text: Consecutive failures usually point at a deterministic issue — a missing tool, a bad prompt, an unresolvable merge conflict. Inspect the execution error before retrying manually.

stale.summary: The card hasn't been updated in a week or more and no execution has touched it recently. It's not blocked by any specific reason — it's just drifted.

callouts.text: Staleness is the fallback reason — we only surface it when nothing else applies. If the card is still worth doing, re-prioritize it; otherwise split it or close it.

slug.summary: The slug is the workspace's permanent URL identifier. You cannot rename it after creation — the entire platform keys off it (routes, API keys, runner configs, prompt overrides).

rows.label: Shape
rows.value: lowercase letters, digits, hyphens — matches /^[a-z0-9-]+$/

rows.label: Where it lives
rows.value: /{slug}/... in every route; /api/workspaces/{slug} in every endpoint

rows.label: Changeable
rows.value: No. Rebuild the workspace if you picked a name you regret.

callouts.text: Pick carefully. Every API key, runner config bundle, prompt override, and bookmarked URL references this slug — there is no rename path.
Creating a workspace with a slug that already exists returns the existing workspace instead of erroring. Safe to retry.

examples: acme-platform, backend-alpha, growth-experiments.
Avoid: ACME_Platform — uppercase and underscores fail validation.

roles.summary: Workspace membership comes in four tiers. Role is set per workspace; a user can be owner of one workspace and viewer of another.

rows.label: owner
rows.value: Full control. Can transfer ownership, delete the workspace, manage billing, and do everything admin can.

rows.label: admin
rows.value: Manage members, edit pipeline config, author prompts, approve high-risk actions, register runners.

rows.label: member
rows.value: Create and edit boards, cards, notes, resources. Cannot edit pipeline config or prompts. Cannot manage members.

rows.label: viewer
rows.value: Read-only across the entire workspace. Can observe runners and activity; cannot mutate anything.

callouts.text: New users are auto-provisioned on first authenticated request. The first member is the creator, provisioned as owner.
The hierarchy is numeric — owner > admin > member > viewer. Endpoints that require admin accept owner; endpoints that require member accept everyone except viewer.

type.summary: Channel type declares how the platform contacts this recipient. Routes outbound notifications — it does not let the recipient push anything back into Backplane.

rows.label: email
rows.value: SMTP address. Used for digests, alert escalations, and stakeholder summaries.

rows.label: slack
rows.value: Slack channel or user ID. Requires workspace-level Slack integration to actually deliver.

rows.label: whatsapp / phone
rows.value: Phone-style address. Delivery is provider-dependent; not all installs have this wired.

rows.label: website / other
rows.value: Free-form URL or label for stakeholder reference — no automated delivery.

callouts.text: Channels are outbound-only. They identify where Backplane should send updates, not where inbound webhooks arrive.
Selecting a type whose transport is not configured on this install means the channel exists but never actually delivers. Check the alert log before assuming the message went out.

contact.summary: The exact address used for outbound delivery. The platform formats notifications to match the channel type but sends to this value verbatim.
examples: email: ops@acme.com
slack: #platform-alerts or U0123ABCD

upload.summary: File uploads use Google Cloud Storage when configured and authenticated local storage otherwise. Files are never exposed as public objects.

rows.label: Backing store
rows.value: GCS when GCS_BUCKET is configured; otherwise LOCAL_STORAGE_DIR behind authenticated routes

rows.label: URL type
rows.value: GCS uses V4 signed URLs; local storage uses authenticated API routes

rows.label: TTL
rows.value: GCS upload URLs expire after 15 minutes and download URLs after 1 hour; local routes have no signed-URL TTL

callouts.text: DELETE removes the Valaris database row, not the underlying object. Bytes remain until a storage lifecycle policy or manual cleanup removes them.
Folders are DB-only constructs for organisation. The underlying GCS path is flat per workspace.

tags.summary: Tags are free-form labels on a resource. The toolbar filter performs case-sensitive textual containment on the stored tag JSON; it does not search file content.
examples: Add via comma or Enter in the resource editor; max 20 tags per resource.
The Backplane editor lowercases and deduplicates tags before saving; API clients should not assume the backend performs that normalization.

callouts.text: The current backend filter is substring-based: selecting `design` can also match `design-system`.

pin.summary: Pinned notes are injected as mandatory context into every runner prompt on this board. This is how you give the LLM instructions it cannot ignore — 'project style is TDD', 'never use any', 'write Spanish error messages for this product'.

rows.label: Scope
rows.value: Workspace notes pin workspace-wide; board notes pin to that board only.

rows.label: Delivery
rows.value: Concatenated into {{.ProjectDirectives}} when a stage has inject_directives: true.

rows.label: Order
rows.value: Pin timestamp ascending — oldest pinned note first. That order shows up in the prompt verbatim.

callouts.text: Directive compliance depends on the model. Opus honors pinned directives reliably; Sonnet drops subtle ones. Pair strict pinned rules with Opus on the stages that must obey them.
Unpinned notes are invisible to runners. They are human-readable context only — useful, but the LLM will not see them.

scope.summary: Notes live at workspace scope or board scope. Workspace notes are visible on every board; board notes stay local to one project.

rows.label: Workspace note
rows.value: Created from /{slug}/notes — appears on every board's Notes tab and feeds board-agnostic runner context.

rows.label: Board note
rows.value: Created from a board's Notes tab — only visible on that board and only pinned to that board's runners.

rows.label: Card note
rows.value: Attached to a single card; surfaces in the card detail sheet. Not pinnable at the prompt-injection layer.

callouts.text: Converting between scopes is not supported — create fresh at the desired scope and delete the original.

fields.summary: Definitions are the board's structured brief. The fields are not decorative — each one feeds a distinct slice of {{.ProjectDirectives}} when a stage injects directives.

sections.title: Objectives / Exclusions
sections.summary: What the project must deliver and what it deliberately will not. Orchestrator reads both before decomposing work into cards; reviewer reads exclusions when judging scope creep.

rows.label: Objectives
rows.value: Outcomes the project is measured by — kept terse; the runner treats each as a claim it must honor.

rows.label: Exclusions
rows.value: Explicit non-goals. 'Not cross-platform; not multi-tenant' keeps runners from wandering.

sections.title: Milestones / Stakeholders
sections.summary: Milestones drive planner stage cadence; stakeholders resolve @-mentions in cards and notes and surface as contact rows for channels.

rows.label: Milestones
rows.value: Dated checkpoints (start, interim, end). Planner uses these to sequence sprints.

rows.label: Stakeholders
rows.value: Humans with a channel. Runners reference them in digests and approval requests.

sections.title: Constraints / Decisions
sections.summary: Constraints are inviolable rules (compliance, budget, tech mandates); decisions are the project's append-only ADR log.

rows.label: Constraints
rows.value: Treated by runners as hard gates — a card violating a constraint should be rejected in review.

rows.label: Decisions
rows.value: Snapshot of historical choices. Useful context when a card implies re-opening a settled question.

callouts.text: Leaving a section empty is fine — runners skip absent fields. Populating a section you will not maintain is worse than leaving it blank.
Constraints written as vague prose get ignored. Imperative, concrete constraints ('Python 3.12 only; no external DNS calls') survive into the runner's output.

scope.summary: Free-form rich-text brief that sits above the structured fields. Think of it as the project's one-pager — the part a human reads first; the structured fields below are the machine-readable slice.

callouts.text: This field is injected into directives too, but unstructured prose is easier for the LLM to drift from. Keep it short or move load-bearing rules into Constraints.

provider.summary: Hint for the platform about how to talk to this host. Today only `github` has working auto-merge and branch-protection plumbing; other providers accept the repo but skip those features.

rows.label: github
rows.value: Full support: gh pr create, auto-merge arming, branch protection via gh api.

rows.label: gitlab / bitbucket / other
rows.value: Repo registered; runners can clone and push, but auto-merge and protection calls are no-ops.

callouts.text: Cross-provider abstraction is on the backlog. Until then, pipelines with reviewer auto-merge should assume GitHub.

branchProtection.summary: When enabled, the runner calls gh api to enforce branch protection on the default branch before shipping — requires PR review, status checks green, no direct pushes.

rows.label: Applies to
rows.value: default_branch of this repo (usually main or master)

rows.label: How
rows.value: gh api PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection — requires a GitHub token with admin scope

rows.label: When
rows.value: Applied each time a runner ships; idempotent — safe to re-apply

callouts.text: Pair with MergeTrigger: on_approve so the reviewer's green light actually gates the merge. Without protection, on_approve is advisory.
GitHub-only today. The flag is stored for other providers but silently does nothing there.

name.summary: Human-readable identifier for this runner. Shown in the runner table, execution logs, and the launch-command filename.
examples: coder-runner, review-runner, secretario — whatever you'd grep for in logs.
Must be unique per workspace. Reusing a name reactivates the existing runner (idempotent create) instead of erroring.

callouts.text: The name becomes the launch-command filename: `runner-<name>.yaml`. Keep it shell-safe — no spaces, no quotes.

description.summary: Optional free-text note about what this runner is for. Shown in the runner detail page; never sent to the LLM.
examples: "Opus, writes code on the billing repo."
"Reviewer-only runner for the planning board."

apiKey.summary: API key the runner uses to authenticate every request. Shown once — copy it now or regenerate later.

callouts.text: Shown once. No recovery. Rotate if you lose it — support cannot retrieve the original.
The prefix is stored server-side for lookup; the secret is hashed at rest. Rotate from the runner detail page and update the runner config when you do.

examples: Paste into the runner's `VALARIS_API_KEY` env var before launching `backplane-runner`.
Rotate on compromise, employee offboarding, or if the key ends up in a screenshot.

allowedWorkspaces.summary: Slugs of workspaces this runner can act in. The create form scopes the runner to the current workspace so it shows up in team pickers and metrics immediately.

rows.label: Default
rows.value: [current workspace slug] — scoped at create time

rows.label: Cross-workspace
rows.value: Add more slugs from the runner detail page after creation

rows.label: Empty list
rows.value: Runner cannot claim or execute anywhere — effectively disabled

callouts.text: Legacy runners may show `null` here. That used to mean "no workspaces," which the metrics filter silently excluded — the operator thought creation failed. The create form now enforces non-empty; if you see null in older runners, backfill with an explicit slug list.
Editing the allowlist is a runner-detail-page operation. The create dialog intentionally limits you to the current workspace to avoid accidentally granting cross-workspace access at onboarding.

launchCommand.summary: Ready-to-paste command that starts the runner. The first line reads the key in without echoing it to your shell history; the second launches with it. Copy, open a terminal, hit enter.
launchCommand.code:
read -s VALARIS_API_KEY && export VALARIS_API_KEY
VALARIS_API_KEY=$VALARIS_API_KEY ./backplane-runner -config runner-<runner>.yaml

callouts.text: Assumes the `backplane-runner` binary is on PATH and a `runner-<name>.yaml` config sits next to it. Export the runner config from the runner detail page if you don't have one yet.

status.summary: Runner liveness is derived by the backend from the last heartbeat; self-reported health is a separate working, idle, or draining signal.

rows.label: alive
rows.value: Last heartbeat is at most 90 seconds old

rows.label: stale
rows.value: Last heartbeat is older than 90 seconds and at most 600 seconds old

rows.label: offline
rows.value: Last heartbeat is older than 600 seconds

rows.label: unknown
rows.value: The Runner has never sent a heartbeat

rows.label: health
rows.value: working, idle, and draining describe Runner activity independently of liveness

callouts.text: Metrics may temporarily promote an in-flight execution started within the last 2 hours to alive even when the latest heartbeat is older.
The UI displays these backend-owned liveness thresholds directly.

healthLastError.summary: Last error the runner self-reported in its health ping. Accessible via hover, focus, or click — not just a mouse-only affordance.

callouts.text: A persistent error here usually means the runner is alive enough to complain but unable to do useful work. Check the runner's own logs for the stack.
The error string is cleared on the next successful operation; it's a snapshot, not a log.

exportConfig.summary: Download the runner's config bundle — `runner-<name>.yaml` plus any referenced prompt files — as a zip. Paste next to your `backplane-runner` binary.

callouts.text: Exported config reflects the runner's current scoping (allowlists, budgets, role). Re-export after editing those fields so the deployed runner picks up the change.

deactivate.summary: Flips the runner's is_active flag off. The runner stops being eligible for new claims; any in-flight execution completes.

callouts.text: Reversible — the Reactivate action flips it back on. Keys are preserved; the runner picks up exactly where it was.
Does not kill the running `backplane-runner` process. Stop the binary on the host if you need the runner gone immediately.

reactivate.summary: Re-enables a previously deactivated runner. Existing API key and allowlist are preserved.

callouts.text: If the `backplane-runner` process is still running on the host, it'll start picking up claims again on its next poll. No restart needed.

addMember.summary: Attach a runner to this team in a specific role. Roles are drawn from the pipeline — adding a role here makes the runner eligible for that role's stages.

callouts.text: Unique-role enforcement: only one runner per role per team. Adding a second runner in the same role replaces the first.
Effective roles on a workspace are the union of all team memberships. A runner can be implementer in Team A and reviewer in Team B simultaneously.

removeMember.summary: Detach this runner from the team. The runner keeps its API key and allowlist; it just won't be eligible for this team's work.

callouts.text: Doesn't affect other team memberships the runner has. Use Deactivate on the runner itself if you want it fully sidelined.

deactivate.summary: Deactivates the team. Members remain attached for audit history but the team stops dispatching work.

callouts.text: In-flight executions belonging to this team continue to completion. Nothing is cancelled mid-run.
Reversible from the team detail page. Consider this when you want to pause a pipeline without tearing down its membership.

roleAssignment.summary: Roles a runner fills on this team. Drawn from the pipeline definition — adding a custom role requires editing the pipeline first.

rows.label: orchestrator
rows.value: Plans and decomposes; never writes code

rows.label: implementer
rows.value: Primary-owner role — owns a card end-to-end, writes code, opens PRs

rows.label: reviewer
rows.value: Collaborator role — reads PRs, emits approve/request_changes

rows.label: documentator
rows.value: Collaborator role — writes release notes, attaches board notes

callouts.text: Assigning a role that isn't in the active pipeline shows a warning triangle on the member chip — the role is valid but won't get scheduled until the pipeline includes a matching stage.

successRate.summary: Completed executions divided by total executions, as a percentage. Rolled up across all workspaces the runner touches.

rows.value: Healthy (green badge)
Degraded (amber badge)
Broken (red badge) — investigate

callouts.text: Zero executions shows 0% by convention, not a divide-by-zero. A fresh runner will always look broken until it ships its first card.
Skipped runs (no prompt, budget exceeded, claim refused) don't count. Only completed + failed feed this ratio.

avgDuration.summary: Average wall-clock duration of a completed execution, in seconds. LLM thinking + tool calls + post-processing, end-to-end.

callouts.text: Averaged over all completed executions ever recorded for this runner — not a rolling window. Long-lived runners will see this smooth out over time.
Failed executions are excluded from the average. A runner that times out a lot will look fast here.

runnerVar.summary: A value the runner substitutes at launch. The five names are declared by the server, not by this screen.

callouts.text: A name the server does not declare renders as an empty string. The prompt still runs, silently missing that value.

examples: {{.Workspace}}
{{.BoardID}}
{{- .Iteration}}

rows.label: Where they come from
rows.value: The palette lists whatever the backend reports.

slot.summary: A placeholder this template fills in when a board binds it.

rows.label: Grammar
rows.value: <<NAME>> — uppercase letter first, then letters, digits or underscores

rows.label: Required
rows.value: A required slot with no value stops the render rather than producing a half-filled prompt

rows.label: Why uppercase and bracketed
rows.value: So a prompt can still contain shell heredocs like `cat <<EOF`.

examples: <<RUN_LABEL>>
<<REPO_URL>>

unknownSlot.summary: This looks like a slot, but no such name exists in the template's catalog.

callouts.text: Either add the slot to the catalog or correct the spelling before publishing.

rows.label: What happens
rows.value: Nothing ever replaces it — the literal text reaches the agent.

max_iterations.summary: Hard ceiling on iterations. The run stops on reaching it whether or not the objective is done — a backstop, not a plan.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Maximum number of agent sessions this run may start.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A runaway loop is bounded by process count, not just by spend.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness, before each iteration; hitting it disables the loop.

examples: 20: about a dozen cards plus headroom for splits and follow-ups.

budget_usd.summary: Cumulative spend cap since the budget epoch. Reaching it ends the run the way the iteration ceiling does.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Total USD this run may spend across every session.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Spend, not iteration count, is what actually bounds an unsupervised run.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness, from the provider rate sheet, before each iteration.

callouts.text: The effective per-session ceiling is the lower of what remains here and the runner's own $30 session cap, so one bad session cannot drain the run.

examples: 250: a multi-phase program over several dozen cards.

max_consecutive_failures.summary: Breaker: this many failed iterations in a row disables the loop. A success anywhere resets the count.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Consecutive failed iterations tolerated before the loop stops.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A loop failing the same way forever should stop and be looked at.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness, after each iteration's outcome is recorded.

callouts.text: Loop #4/#5 taught this: an objective_complete the completion query refutes counts as a FAILED iteration and burns the breaker, so never claim it unchecked.

links.label: Loop mode: knowing why it stopped

iteration_timeout_seconds.summary: Wall-clock ceiling for one session. A timeout is recorded as a FAILED iteration, so it burns the breaker.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Seconds a single agent session may run before it is cut.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Whole-feature cards need a long session; a wedged one must still end.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness; a cut session's uncommitted work is lost.

callouts.text: Loop #7 raised this to 5400s because whole-feature cards outgrew the 3600s default — and because a cut session loses anything not yet pushed.

examples: 5400: ninety minutes, for cards that span backend and frontend.

iteration_delay_seconds.summary: Cooldown between one session ending and the next starting. Also the base of the park backoff.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Seconds the harness waits before it wakes the next session.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Board writes settle, and a parked loop backs off instead of spinning.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness between iterations, and the parking chain.

examples: 60: the default cadence for a whole-feature run.

max_blocked_on_human.summary: How many consecutive parks on an operator decision are tolerated before the loop disables itself. 0 opts out.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Consecutive blocked_on_human outcomes before the loop stops.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Nobody is watching; parking forever is indistinguishable from hanging.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness; below the threshold the loop parks with backoff.

callouts.text: Loop #6 taught this: an unsupervised run must name its blocker and stop, rather than park silently until the budget runs out.

links.label: Loop mode: knowing why it stopped

starvation_policy.summary: What the loop does when no card is workable: park at zero cost, or wake anyway and re-check.

rows.label: What
rows.value: park — idle until something changes; always_run — start a session regardless.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A dependency-heavy board is mostly blocked early; parking costs nothing.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The harness, when the discovery query returns no eligible card.

examples: park: the default for a board whose cards unblock each other.

loop_landing.summary: Where the loop's merges land: a human owns the merge, or the platform merge queue does.

rows.label: What
rows.value: human — no platform merge queue; merge_queue — the platform lands it.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A self-landing loop merges its own branches and needs no queue.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The merge executor, and the agent-enqueue gate.

callouts.text: Under human landing a self-improve run merges its own card branches into its integration branch with plain git; promoting that branch to main stays the operator's decision.

merge_gate.summary: Which CI verdict the merge executor consults before landing a queued entry.

rows.label: What
rows.value: forge_ci — require the forge's checks; none — land without consulting them.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A queued merge should not land over a red build.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The platform merge executor, per queued entry.

callouts.text: Under human landing this never fires for the loop itself: only agent enqueues are rejected, and a self-landing loop never enqueues.

model.summary: Which model the sessions run on — a tier alias the runner resolves, or a concrete model id passed through verbatim.

rows.label: What
rows.value: premium, mid or low, or any provider model id.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Card difficulty, not habit, should pick the tier.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The runner at launch, via its tier-to-provider mapping.

examples: premium: whole-feature cards that span several layers.
mid: mechanical or single-file cards.

provider.summary: Which agent backend runs the sessions. Left empty, the runner uses the provider its tier mapping names.

rows.label: What
rows.value: A free-form provider name, never a closed vocabulary.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: The platform stays white-label; the runner owns provider policy.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The runner at launch, when resolving the model tier.

examples: Empty: take whatever the runner's tier mapping resolves.

system_prompt.summary: Sent once as the agent's system prompt. Slots render at bind time; runner variables render every iteration.

rows.label: What
rows.value: The engagement: repo, boundaries, what must never be touched.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Standing rules belong where they cannot be crowded out mid-run.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The runner, once per session, before the loop prompt.

loop_prompt.summary: Sent every iteration. The runner appends its tools manifest after rendering.

rows.label: What
rows.value: The method: how to pick a card, do the work, and stop.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A fresh session needs the procedure restated every time.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The runner, at the start of each iteration.

callouts.text: An edit here applies from the NEXT iteration — the harness re-fetches the config every cycle, so no restart is needed.

required_column_types.summary: Column types the board MUST have before this template can run. A missing one is a fit error, not a warning.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Column types the fit check treats as mandatory.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A loop that moves cards needs somewhere to move them to.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, before a board may bind this template.

callouts.text: These are column TYPES (backlog, active, review, done, blocked), not column names — a board may call its active column anything.

optional_column_types.summary: Column types the template can use if present. Absence is reported as advice, never as a blocking fit error.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Column types that improve the fit but are not required.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A template should degrade gracefully on a simpler board.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, as a warning rather than an error.

requires_run_label.summary: The loop only picks up cards carrying the run's label, so one board can host a run without swallowing its whole backlog.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Whether card discovery is scoped to a run label.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Unlabelled backlog and other people's work must stay out of reach.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The discovery query, and the completion query that ends the run.

callouts.text: The same label defines when the run is DONE: no labelled card left outside a done column.

git_repo_bound.summary: The board must have a git repo bound, because the loop clones it and pushes card branches.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Whether a bound repository is a precondition.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Without a repo the agent has nowhere to land the work it describes.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, and the runner when it prepares a workspace.

agent_bound_with_tools.summary: An agent must be bound AND granted tools — including the off switch, or the loop cannot stop itself.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Whether a tool-granted agent binding is a precondition.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A loop with no way to disable itself has to be killed by hand.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, and the harness off-switch pre-flight.

callouts.text: A bind is rejected while enabled when set_board_loop is absent from the grant — the loop would have no way to report that it is finished.

links.label: Loop mode: knowing why it stopped

dependencies_server_side.summary: Card order comes from server-computed dependencies, not from prose in the card body.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Whether the run relies on wired card dependencies.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A fresh session cannot infer order; the server must hand it one.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The discovery query, which skips cards whose prerequisites are open.

callouts.text: Both ready and unblocked mean workable — ready has no prerequisites, unblocked has all of them satisfied. Only blocked excludes a card.

definition_keys.summary: Keys the board definition must carry for this template — the constitution the agent re-reads every iteration.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Definition sections the template expects to find.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: The definition outranks every card; a missing key removes a rule.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, and the agent on every iteration.

pinned_notes.summary: Notes the board must have pinned — the seed batch, the spec, whatever a fresh session has to find on its own.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Pinned notes this template's prompts refer to by title.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A session with no memory finds context only where it is pinned.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, and the agent when it orients.

card_sections.summary: Headings every card body should carry, so a session reads the same contract on every card.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Section headings the template's prompts expect in a card.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A card missing its acceptance criteria is a card the agent must guess at.

rows.label: Used by
rows.value: The fit check, and the agent when it reads the card.

examples: Acceptance Criteria
Test-First DoD
Out of Scope

name.summary: The identifier the prompts reference as <<NAME>>. Upper snake case only — the publish validator rejects anything else.

rows.label: What
rows.value: The slot's `<<NAME>>` token, matched literally in both prompts.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: Renaming here does not rewrite the prompts — the slot goes unused until you update them too.

examples: RUN_LABEL
MAX_RETRIES

kind.summary: How the value is typed and validated. Single line rejects newlines; the others each get their own editor below.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Single line, Multi-line text, Choice list, Preset, or List of lines.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: The kind is the wire contract: a newline inside a single-line slot fails render with scalar_must_be_single_line.

required.summary: A required slot must be filled before a board can bind this template. Optional slots fall back to their default.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Blocks binding while the slot is empty and has no default.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: It moves the failure to bind time, where an operator can fix it, instead of mid-run.

autofill.summary: Fills the slot from board state at bind time, so the operator never retypes something the platform already knows.

rows.label: What
rows.value: A named source the binder reads — board id, workspace slug, repo, and friends.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: An autofilled slot still accepts an explicit value; the operator's entry wins.

default.summary: The value used when the operator leaves the slot empty. Its shape follows the kind — a list default is an array.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Pre-fills the bind form and satisfies an optional slot on its own.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: A default is stored as authored: a list stays a list, never flattened into one string.

variant.summary: A preset is one named choice that fills several slots at once, so related settings move together.

rows.label: What
rows.value: Each preset carries a map of slot to value, applied when the operator picks it.

rows.label: Why
rows.value: An operator's own entry for a slot beats the preset's fill for that slot.

reasonNeedsAdvisor.title: Parked — needs an advisor

reasonNoHero.title: No primary owner assigned

reasonRequestChanges.title: A review requested changes
reasonRequestChanges.body: The latest review decision parsed from the card is `request_changes`. The card's owner needs to address the feedback — typically a rework commit — before the review can re-run and the PR can merge.

reasonRecentFailures.title: {{count}} recent execution failed
reasonRecentFailures.body: Consecutive failures trigger the scheduler's failure backoff. If the card doesn't recover on the next tick, inspect the execution error and either fix the underlying issue or route the card through `on_failure.move_to_column_type`.

reasonStale.title: No activity in {{days}} days
reasonStale.body: No execution has touched this card recently and it isn't in Done. If none of the other reasons apply, the card may be waiting on a missing dependency or simply drifted — re-prioritize or split it.

rolesGlossary.title: Roles
rolesGlossary.subtitle: What each role does, when it runs, and how it differs from the others. The defaults below describe the conventional pipeline — you can rename, delete, or add roles freely in the pipeline builder.

orchestrator.name: Orchestrator
orchestrator.headline: Decomposes objectives into cards and sequences the pipeline.
orchestrator.whenToUse: Start of a fresh project, after a major re-scope, or when the backlog has drifted from the north star.

implementer.name: Implementer
implementer.headline: Writes the code. Claims a card, cuts a branch, ships a PR.
implementer.whenToUse: Every card that changes code. This is the highest-spend role — always pair with your strongest model.

reviewer.name: Reviewer
reviewer.headline: Inspects an open PR and emits approve or request_changes.
reviewer.whenToUse: After the implementer opens a PR. Structured-output decision gates auto-merge; directive compliance matters — prefer Opus.

documentator.name: Documentation owner
documentator.headline: Records what shipped as a card note for humans and downstream runners.
documentator.whenToUse: After merge, or whenever a card reaches Done. Keeps institutional memory alive without blocking the critical path.

planner.name: Planner
planner.headline: Splits oversized cards, orders sprints, re-prioritizes the backlog.
planner.whenToUse: Before a sprint, after scope changes, or when discover strategies are starving for claimable work.

researcher.name: Researcher
researcher.headline: Gathers external context — docs, prior art, API refs — and attaches notes.
researcher.whenToUse: Before implementation when the card touches an unfamiliar library, a new API, or a domain with heavy prior art.

mcpOnboarding.title: Connect your coding agent
mcpOnboarding.subtitle: Give your agent authenticated access to this workspace over MCP.
mcpOnboarding.introHeading: Your agent, working on this board
mcpOnboarding.introBody: Backplane exposes dozens of platform tools — boards, cards, notes, approvals, executions and more — over the Model Context Protocol. Any MCP-capable agent, whether that is Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or something you built on an SDK, can read this workspace and plan, file and move real work on this kanban.
mcpOnboarding.introPromise: We'll get you connected in three short steps.
mcpOnboarding.positioningIntro: Two different things run on this platform, and you only need the first one today.
mcpOnboarding.positioningMcpBody: Interactive. Your own Claude Code or Codex session reads and writes the board while you steer it — you ask, it files the card, moves it, leaves the note.
mcpOnboarding.positioningRunnersBody: Autonomous Go pipelines that pick up cards on their own through next_assignment, using this same MCP tool surface under tool policies the backend enforces per pipeline stage.
mcpOnboarding.positioningCoexistence: The same board serves both. The cards you file and refine in your session are the cards a runner can execute later.
mcpOnboarding.positioningNoRunnerNeeded: You do not need a runner to use MCP. Everything in this wizard works with your own agent session alone.
mcpOnboarding.keyIntro: Your agent authenticates with a platform API key.
mcpOnboarding.keyIdentityHint: The name you give the key is the identity shown in activity history whenever the key acts, so pick something you'll recognise months from now.
mcpOnboarding.keyRevealWarning: This is the only time the full key is shown. Copy it before you continue — you won't see it again.
mcpOnboarding.keyExistingHeading: Use a key you already have
mcpOnboarding.keyExistingHint: Existing keys can't be shown again, so if you pick one you'll paste it into the next step yourself.
mcpOnboarding.connectIntro: Paste this message into your agent to configure its connection. In the next step, check authentication activity and run a read-only native-tool check.
mcpOnboarding.connectSubstituteHint: Replace the placeholder with the full key you saved. Existing keys can't be revealed again — create a new key if you no longer have it.
mcpOnboarding.connectAdvancedIntro: This is a fresh local stdio setup, even when the Backplane API is remote. Merge it into your existing configuration, preserving custom toolsets and any allowlist. For remote MCP HTTP, the server operator configures and restarts the service.

mcpOnboarding.verifyNextBulk: Describe a sprint in a paragraph and let the agent file the whole backlog at once.
mcpOnboarding.verifyNextDocsBody: Browse the full tool catalog, grouped by what each tool does, without leaving Backplane.

mcpOnboarding.verifyAuthHistoricalBody: Previous key activity was recorded. This historical evidence does not verify your current agent connection or native tools.
mcpOnboarding.verifyToolCheckPending: Native tool check pending — tool availability is not independently verified by this wizard.
mcpOnboarding.verifyResultReported: You reported that the agent check succeeded. This is not independently verified by Backplane; it covers only the calls the agent actually made.
mcpOnboarding.verifyRecoveryMissingTools:
For missing native tools, use the exact returned restart_env when available, preserving every enabled group, including custom groups. Keep all allowlists intact. Preset configuration is an example for a fresh connection, not a replacement for existing configuration.

For local stdio, apply it to the MCP server launch environment, even if the Backplane API is remote. For remote MCP HTTP, ask the operator to apply it to the remote server environment; local client environment changes cannot configure that service.

Restart the MCP server/connection, then start a fresh agent session and rerun the check. A new chat alone can reuse a stale catalog; repeating enable_toolsets alone may not refresh it.
mcpOnboarding.verifyRecoveryAuth: Check the configured API key and authorized workspace access with the operator. Confirm the credential is active and has the required permissions; toolset selection cannot grant access. Do not paste credentials into the check or remove authorization restrictions.
mcpOnboarding.verifyRecoveryNetwork: Check network connectivity and the configured URL or endpoint. For local stdio, check that the MCP process can reach the Backplane API; for remote HTTP, check that the client can reach the MCP service and the service can reach Backplane. Ask the operator to inspect service availability.
mcpOnboarding.verifyRecoveryVersionAllowlist: Compare the installed MCP server version with the documented tools, and ask the operator to inspect configured toolsets and allowlists. A selected preset cannot bypass an allowlist; preserve it and resolve any version or authorized configuration mismatch before restarting the server/connection and rerunning the check.
